PROSECUTION OF GAS STOKERS.
DUTY OP TRA.DES SOCIETIES.
The trades unionists throughout the king-
dom have just received a challenge which they
must not refuse to accept. The middle and
upper classes of England have always regarded
their proceedings with aversion and dread. ,
Combinations amongst the working men of
England for any purpose, however laudable,
are suspected of ultimate objects unfavourable
to ordinary class denomination ; and hence
combination laws, and other disabling re-
strictions, as ill•intentioned in spirit as they
have been injurious and degrading to those
against whom they were levelled.
The struggles which working men have been
making to get out of the embarrassing position
in which they have been thus placed by the
law have now gone on for years, and every
attempt by the Legislature to liberate them has
been made in suh a grudging and suspicious
spirit, that much of the old bondage remains,
and here and there new. links have been
rivetted on to the old chain, which impede and
gall as badly as if forged in the "good old"
tim es.

The Gas Stokers' strike, and the conse-
quence it has drawn after, force this matter
most urgently on the attention of the trades
unionists of the country ;—in fact, in such a
way that they must take it up and fight it out
fairly in the courts if they would understand
the ground they actually occupy before the
law ;—if, in fact, they would know whether
the men who conduct their affairs are acting
legally and safely should they decide upon a
strike as necessary, or whether they are liable
to be dragged before the judges of the land, and
condemned to the fate of felons as conspirators.
For those who have been condemned under
the old law of master and servant little
can be done. In this matter the law
must be altered. It is a criminal act
on the part of a hired person to leave
his employment without the understood
notice, though it is not a criminal act on the
part of the employer to turn his men away.
The law, as it exists, is a one-sided, degrading '
law—a law that would have been repealed long
ago if working men had not in them some
portion of the slave's submissiveness. But se
long as it remains, and the disposition to
enforce it exists, there is no use in grumbling
about it. The gas stokers say that a week's
notice when men are discharged is not given
as a rule. They are, they say, habitually dis-
charged at any hour and under any pretence.
This practice, however, does not justify the
men, nor do they appear to have regarded it
as a justification. Not having their union
thoroughly organized, they" acted on the provo-
cation given at the instant. They saw men

But the right understanding of such a
matter is the very last thing the public press
will seek to promote. Acts of folly or of
violence on the part of trades unionists find
ample record, and furnish admirable texts for
sermons in the columns of our newspapers on
the dangers of trades' combinations ; but the
quiet, orderly management of these bodies, by
which conflicting interests are reconciled, and
forethought and provident habits encouraged,
are not perceived by our public writers. The
careful management of large corporate affairs,
by which working men's intellectual faculties
are exercised and their moral powers increased,
only tends to bring the best and most active
men under suspicion with the general public,
and more within the reach of the law which,
in the baseness of vulgar selfish suspicion,
arms itself with penalties and punishments
against them.
The errors and accidents connected with the
Stokers' strike must, at the present moment,
be put completely on one side, and the one
clear issue raised. Is it conspiracy to counsel
a strike? Are those who manage trades
societies, in the exercise of their ordinary
duties, liable to be charged, convicted, and
punished as conspirators? Let this be tried
now and settled once for all in the ease now
before the courts; and. whatever funds are
necessary for this purpo6e should be promptly
and liberally furnished. But, which over way
the decision el the court may go, the position
of working men should not be allowed to re-
main what it is. The next Trades Con-
gress, soon about to meet at Leeds, should
draw up a spirited remonstrance against what-
ever injurious inequality the law contains in
regard to the workers of the country. The
masters' and servants' law should not be
allowed to continue what it is. Broach of
contract on the part of the man, as well
as on the part of the master, shout' be
treated simply as a civil offence; whilst
everything as special offence and punishment
provides for by the Criminal Law Amendment
Act, and all such exceptional one-sided
legislation should be methodically, persever
ingly, and actively agitated against, until the
law shall contain no provision which marks
the working man with a brand of inferiority,
or singles him out for special punishment as an
exceptionally dangerous member of the com-
munity. It is not tinkering that is needed in
this matter, but a clean sweep that shall wipe
out old oppressions and disgraces.

made to Mr. Justice I3Errr for a postponement
of the trial of the committed men has been re-

TIIE INCOME TAX.

IT is full time that there should be in the
House of Commons real representatives of the
working classes. The meeting last week in
the Guildhall proves the necessity of this.
Who composed this meeting? The speakers
and assistants were one and all of the moneyed
class—of that class which may be styled the
plutocracy in distinction to the landed aria-
tooraoy, and who are the great employers of
labour.

_
Now, what was the object of this meeting,
with the LORD MATOR at its head? It was
simply, I maintain, to take off taxation from its
own class and place it upon the working
classes. There are two species of taxation—
direct and indirect. The indirect taxes are chiefly
those on consumption, suoh as the taxes on
beer, tobacco, tea, coffee, sugar, &a. Those tax( ss
are paid principally by the masses—the work-
ing classes. To give an equivalent for this,
and equalize, in some degree, the burden of
taxation betwixt the rich and poor, according
to the respective means of each, an Income
Tax was introduced by Sir ROBERT NEL in
1841. The Income Tax has been continued
ever since with great success, and has enabled
the Legislature to diminish the taxes upon
the necessaries of life. Against this system of
taxation the capitalists of the Guildhall meet-
ing have raised their protest, which is to be
followed out by all their influence in the
house of Commons. They wish the Income
Tax not to be modified or improved in its de-
tail, but to be done entirely away with, and
its place filled up by an increase in the taxes
on tea, sugar, tlbacco, beer, ttc. They do
not, it is true, in their resolutions, directly say
that the indirect taxes are to be increased.
They suggest that by proper economy the
National Expenditure might be diminished by
six millions—the amount raised by the In-
come Tax—and that by this saving the whole
Income Tax might be dispensed with. This
comes exactly to the same thing ; for if a
saving is made in the National Expenditure,
that saving ought to be applied to the diminu-
tion of the burdens on the working classes,
and not exclusively—as the meeting in Guild-
hall resolved—to the abolition of the Income
Tax.

The food, the clothing, and the lodging of

CIUUSTOPIIEIt NEvILE.

PROGRESS.
No. 11.

TILE conception of progress is the result of a
vast progress already accomplished. It was
not till the middle of the 17th century that it
became the subject of vigorous speoulation ;
and even then the knowledge and intellect of
mankind had not advanced sufficiently to
allow of the formation of adequate ideas of
progress—even then the most powerful minds
ware quite incapable of seeing that the move-
ment, which was obscrved, was a continuous
advance towards perfection. Vice, an eminent
Italian philosopher, who lived at the end of

the 17th century, who treated social pheno-
mena with great breadth of view and origin.-
ality, thought that the human movement must
be circular. It was a great step to recognise
that there was movement. I3ut the other
ideas which the conception of progreasinvOves,
such as growth, organization, development,
law, could only be evolved With the gradual
advance of science. Many a noble life had
first to be devoted to the pursuit of philosophy
and science, to the, physical sciences, to the
science of vegetable and animal life, and to
that of social existence. How much, too, had
to be altered and destroyed? How many of
the fictions of our childhood had to be given
up, those dreams round which habit and
affection stilt make so many of its cling? Men
were obliged, by force of fact, to acknowledge
that there was no such thing as chance; that
there was no disorder; that there was no
arbitrary interference of any sort or kind, and
never had been; but that from the beginning
to the end there has been one universal order
subject to invariable natural laws, one uni-
formity of nature exhibiting regularity even
where events:appear most irregular and capri-
cious. This invariable order which, Underlies
all. things, however variable-they may seem to
be—this constancy in the midst of apparthit
inconstancy, whether it be of such phenomena
as the winds, or the changing currents of

ought and feeling, is, in truth and in fact,

the primary condition of progress. If it, were
not so, we ebould be living in a different
world, if there was no such constancy—if

I we could not be certain that the same effects
would follow the same causes, as, for example,
that fire would boil water, or that a certain
pressure upwards would counteract the same
pressure downwards—if we were not sure that
what is true to-day will be true to-morrow—
if we could not foresee the result of our actions
—if experience went for nought—if everything
had to be tried afresh, and every new trial was
equally worthless, then all dependence, con-
viction, reliance, certainty, and hope would be
gone. Happily, however, there is no doubt and
no choice about it. The fixity of the natural
order, and the invariability of the highest
laws, is a settled and acknowledged fact. It
is proved by the largest proof and most com-
plete verification that man can have, namely,
by the universal experience of mankind
throughout the past. The scientific or positive
fact that the whole universe, and that all
phenomena are subordinate to invariable
natural laws, is the only possible foundation
of consistent purpose and persistent conduct.
This is the first condition of progress.

But it may well be asked by those who have
never followed out this train of thought, Is not
this a kind of fatalism? I answer no, just
the opposite. As well might you call the
fixed point or fulcrum of the lever fatalism.
In both cases the fixity is the condition of
action. There has been, for many ages, a
great dispute in the schools of thought about
Tree-will and necessity; but when viewed from
the positive or scientific standpoint it is a dis-
pute of words and empty wind. But it may
still be urged if this fixity is not fatalism, are
there not phenomena which are altogether
beyond our power? Yes, there are many.
For example, the astronomical events, such
as the movements of the planets and stars,
are beyond our power. And if all phenomena

were similarly out of our reach we could do
nothing i that would be fatalism; progress
would be impossible. This brings me to the
second condition of progress. Although there
are many phenomena over which we cannot
exercise any control, there are many more that
are capable of being modified. The first con-
dition of progress is the fixity and invariability
of the highest laws; the second condition is
that phenomena can be moulded for man's
advantage. Science has always two objects in
view. The knowledge of scientific laws gives
us two powers,; first, that of prevision, or the
power of foretelling events ; secondly, the
power of modifying events. And it is a great
truth of philosophy, that tne less the one power
the greater is the other. That is to say, when
the events are simple and general, they admit
of being predicted with great certainty and
precision. • The more complicated they are,
the more difficult it is to foretell with exact-
ness What will happen; but then, as a conse-
quence, and as a compensation for this defi-
ciency, this very complexity gives us greater
power of introducing alterations, and of re-
pairing the grievous imperfections by which
we are surrounded. Thus our very difficulties
Impose upon us as a necessary duty the im-
provement of ourselves and of our situation,
and at the same time afford us the means of
doing so successfully. In astronomy, where
we are quite powerless to alter, our power of
prevision is at its higheit. It is well known
with what accuracy astronomers foretell
eclipses, the appearance of comets, and the
like. The exact correspondence of the occur-
rence of such Oents with the predictions of
astronomy naturally impresses every mind with
the certainty and truth of the science by which
men are able so to dip into the future. The
ancient superstition, which attributes the
occurrence of such things as comets and
eclipses to supernatural and capricious agen-
cies, crumbles away, and the noble conception
of regularity replaces that o arbitrary will.
The practical value of the
power of prevision
is, that where we know that something is
inevitable, we can adjust ourselves to it, we
can make our arrangemects and preparations,
avoid dangers, and take advantage of the
opportunities which our knowledge affords us.
Our whole life is a succession of examples of
this prevision, based upon 'experience. The 1

se we make' of the tides, our preparations for

the return of the sevons, or for the succession
of d.ny and night, are examples of tilts. Thus
then, although there are many inevitable evils

to which we must always be content to be re-
signed, although our oWn nature is very weak
and imperfect, and the imperfection of the
material world in which we live is no lees
striking, yet, nevertheless, this very imperf"-
ti.on is the reason why there is so vast a field
for human exertion, so vast as to give man an
unlimited scope for perpetual improvement
the opportunity of constantly striving toward s
a higher perfection. When I say, then, that
resignation is a duty, I do not mean that
in should be a passive, fatalistic, degrading'
but an active, intelligent, ennobling resigna-
tion.

The old dispitte of free will and necessity
vanishes before the positive coneeptions ef
the fixity of the natural order and the power
the first and second conditions of progress,
of modifying secondary phenomena. These are
the
reason why man has hitherto progressed, and
the mode in which he will continue to do Se.
The magnificent spectacle of the regularitY f
the movements of the heavenly bodies, las ;
more than ought else suggested to mankind
the splendid idea of universal order. But that
alone would have been but one-half of the
truth. The impossibility of our altering those
events would have led us straight to fatalism/
had we not been able to supply the other
half of the truth from another source,
namely, from those phenomena which
their complexity have allowed and even forced
us into practical action, and especially from
the phenomena of life. From such a source
and from the successful struggle of man against
the miseries and imperfections of his lot, from
the actual reaction of man against nccessitio
rose The idea of progress.
These two great facts, of order and progress;
are fundamental; they are necessary to tdl
true conceptions either of human nature or Of
the world in which we live. Each of them has
formed the basis of different schools of thought. ,
They have been regarded as inconsistent alld
antagonistic. Even now, used in a veil
narrow sense, it is a common expression of the
present political writings to speak of Conser-
vatives as "the friends of order," and the
Radicals as "the party of progress." AUGUSTE
COMTE, who is, in my opinion, the wisest and ,
most profound thinker that has ever lived, in
his great works on Social Science has showed
that 80 far from order being opposed to pro-
gress, they depend mutually upon each other,
and are, in reality, but different aspects of the
same truth. He has, by demonstration, satis-
factorily reconciled order and progress. There
can be no true order where there is no pro-
gress. Order is .the condition of progress,
while progress is the end and object of .
order.

articles.title: GAS STOK.ERS' STRIKE.
articles.text:
THE GAS STOK.ERS' STRIKE.

THE PROSECUTIONS.

lohn Bunn, George Ray, Robert Wilson, Ed-
grind Jones, and Thomas William Dilley were
placed in the dock, and indicted for conspiring to
. intimidate George Charles Trewby, the manager of
the Beekton Gas Works of the Gas Light and Coke
Company.
lir. Gifford, Q.C., was specially retained, with
Mr. Bealey, to conduct the prosecution ; Mr.
Montagu Williams, Mr. Straight, Mr. Humph-
reys, and Mr. Matthews were council for the
prisoners.
The offence imputed to the defendants was varied
in different counts, in one of which they were
charged with intending to place the streets of the
metropolis in darkness by cutting off the supply of
pa to the various local autho rides:
, In opening the case, Mr. Gifford observed that
it would be affectation to suppose that the jury
Were not aware of the circumstances under which
the 500 men suddenly left the Beckton Gas Works.
It appeared that one of the defendants, Dilley,
Was discharged from his employment for insubor-
dination, and thereupon the other men endeavoured
to procure his reinstatement, and they evidently
believed that if their demand were not ccmplied
with the streets of London would at once be placed
in darkness by their suddenly ceasing from
Continuing to perform their work. Undoubtedly,
the consequences of such a course of conduct were
calculated to be of a very serious character, and
Mr. Trewby, the manager, said he would restore
Daley under protest. The men next required that
two men who had been discharged at Fulham
should also be reinstated, but. Mr. Trewby said it
was impossible for him to comply with this request,
as the men bad been in the service of another
company. The defendants then represented that
their union required them to leave work unless the
Fulham men were restored, and they accordingly
—the whole 500 workmen—left in a body at half
past six, although they were at this time under a
contract, by the terms of which they could only
leave the service of the company after giving due
notice. They had, therefore, clearly conspired
to break their contracts aud intiinidate the

company.
Some techincal objections were then taken by
the counsel for the defendants to the form of the
indictment ; but they were all overruled by the

court,
The defence set up for the .prisoners was, that
they did not know that they were acting contrary

to law.
Mr. Justice Brett summed up the evidence at
considerable length.
The Jury retired at 20 minutes to five o'clock
to deliberate, and fhey returned into court a little
before five, and found all the defendants Guilty,
but strongly recommended them to mercy, on
account of their great ignorance and being misled.
The learned Judge said he was sorry to see men
who appeared to have borne good characters
convicted of such an offance, but the evidence left
the jury no alternative. Their offence might
have been attended with the most dangerous con-
sequences, and he felt it his duty to sentence them
to be imprisoned and kept to hard labour for
twelve months. •

articles.title: LONDON CARPENTERS AND
articles.text:
THE LONDON CARPENTERS AND

JOINERS.

An important case (Jepps v. Joaolyn) was
heard at Southwark County Court, before Mr.
Whitmore, on the 10th inst. The plaintiff sued
for is. 7d., being a deficiency of id. per hour for
thirty-nine hours worked. The defendant, having
a class of men working for him for a id. per hour
less than the standard wages, declared he was not
bound to comply with the late advance of wages.
in oonsequence of the strike, as he was no party
to the transaction of the Masters' Association.
The Judge quite concurred with the demand of
the plaintiff, and said that no master builder could
plead ignorance of the fact, and remarked that he
had no doubt the defendant could get men to
work for 7d. per hour, but nevertheless it was his
duty to make the agreement to that effect, and
his Honour granted the plaintiff the amount
claimed with cost and expenses, in all 7s. H.,
much to the chagrin of the defendant.

articles.title: MASTER BUILDERS OF
articles.text:
THE MASTER BUILDERS OF

LONDON.

The association which was formed last summer,
in consequence of the strike of the building opera-
tives, held a general meeting at the Westminster
Palace Hall on Tuesday evening last, for the pur-
pose of adopting rake for tho permanent consti-
tution of the association, the aka of which is set
forth as follows

The object of the association will be the promo-
tion and protection of the interests of the building
trade of London generally, and of the members of
the association in particular, by the following
amongst other means :

Ist. Unity of action in the settlement of all ques-
lions arising between employers and their workmen,
with a view to prevent lock-outs or unjust strikes
against individual members of the association.
2nd. The general adoption of equitable condi-
tions of contract such as those recently agreed to
by the Royal Institute of British Architects.
3rd. The interchange of information and mutual
co-operation when desirable with other kindred
societies throughout the country.
4th. The collection and circulation among its
members of statistics and other information con-
sidered to be for the general interests of the trade.
• bth. The keeping a register at the offices of the
association, of foremen and others who can be re-
commended for employment.
The rules were unanimously ` adopted, and a
permanent committee of 21 leading members of the
trade was elected by ballot, with ample powers to
att for the general welfare, and with power to call
an aggregate meeting whenever a strike against
any member shall be threatened.

articles.title: TB BI.RiaNdITAN CARPENTERS.
articles.text:
TB BI.RiaNdITAN CARPENTERS.

A meeting of the Amalgamated and General
Union of Carpenters was held on Thursday night
in the Temperance Hall, Birmingham, for the
purpose of considering a new code of rules sub-
mitted by the committee. Mr. J. Loughton occu-
pied the chair.
Mr. Makepeace, the secretary, submitted the
revised code of rules, which were afterwards taken
seriatim. The first rule submitted was to the effect
that the hours of labour should extend from 7 a.m.
to 5 p.m. on the first five days of the week, with
anhour and a half for meals, except Saturday,
when the time of leaving off should be at one
o'clock, with half an hour for breakfast; this
arrangement to extend all the year round. Two
amendments were moved, one of which was with-
drawn; and the other, moved by Mr. Archer,

WaS
That the hours extend from 6.30 a.m. to .5 p.m.
on each of the first five days of the week with an
hour and a half for meals; and on Saturdays from
6.30 a.m. to 12 p.m. and half an hour for break-
fast; and from November 13th to February sth,
on exposed buildings, the hours of work be from
7 to 5, with half an hour for breakfast and half an
hour for dinner on the first live days of the week,
and .on Saturdays from 7 to 12 with half an hour
for breakfast.
After some discussion, the original resolution
was carried by a largo majority. ,
The next rule submitted related
,to the rate of
wages, and was to the effect
That the. wagm for skilled workmen be paid
for at the rate of Sid. per hour on and after the Ist
May next, superior or inferior workmen to be
rated by the employers or foremen.
This was passed readily.
The next alteration related to overtime, and was
as follows :
That all overtime made at the request of the
employer, between 5 p.m. and 7 an., and after
1 p.m. on Saturday, to be paid time-and-a-half ;
Sundays double time, ,Worktuen making over-
time at tloir own request, to be paid half-time
only.
This was •al:so passed with little discussion.

The rule governing walking time and lodgings
was made MOTO definite, as follows:

If the job he not more than two miles from
Stephenson-place, the men shall walk back in
their own time. If more than two miles then
walking time Shall be allowed at the rate of three
miles per hour beyond the first mile and a half.
The men shall walk back in their own time except
on Saturdays, when the wages are not paid on the
place ..)f work; lodgings and railway fire to be
paid by employers to all men sent from the town

and workmen.
The rule relating to the liberty of the employer
to please himself in the matter of maehineiy, num-
ber of apprentices, &e., was expunged, and that
relating to the alteration of the rules was fixed
so as to ensure written notice of alteration
to be given by the let of November in any
year, so that any party objecting may have an
opportunity of sending in. a written rejoinder by the

articles.title: CARPENTERS AT BIRKENHEAD.
articles.text:
THE CARPENTERS AT
BIRKENHEAD.

At a recent public meeting of the branch of
the Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and
Joiners, at Birkenhead, the sum of £lOO, accident

articles.text:
BOILERMAKERS A.ND IRON SIIIP

BUILDERS' SOCIETY.

Mr. Knight, the general secretary, in the
November report of the above society says :-.-
WOIt.TILY BROTILERS,---" Political economists
speak slightingly and sneeringly of trade combina,
tions, and deny their utility to us 5.8 workingmen,
but our experience teaches us the contrary, and to
our society we intend to cling as our sheet anchor.
The public have been taught to believe that all
,trades unions are aggressive bodies, only waiting
an opportunity to rob the employer of his legiti-
mate profits by extortionate demands. Nothing is
a greater fallacy. Nine ont of every ten strikes
that take plate are against a reduction of wages, or
against some innovation of an old established rule,
and if we were to allow these encroachments by

the masters on our rights, more important innova-
tions would be attempted. As an illustration of
the value of our soeiety in preventing an evil,
and a proof that strikes are not always a loss, we
will refer you to the Manchester case, as named
in last report. Here was an employer who had
plenty of work, in fact they are so busy that, had

it been summer instead of winter, the men would
have been compelled to work overtime, but because
the days are short, and the mornings very dark,
the manager does not think the men can do as
much before breakfast as in good daylight; he there-
fore proposes that they shall not start until day-
light comes, but he does not propose the men Shall
be paid full time for it. Oh, no; the men must
suffer a reduction in their wages averaging 6s. 6d.
each man per week, and what good would the time
in the morning have been to the men? None in the
least. And no doubt this short time movement would
have continued four months, raalling.a total loss to
the men of ..£5 45., the exact amount oftwo years'
contributions to their society. And this undoubt-
edly they would have had to submit to had there
been none in existence. And no doubtthis move-
ment would have extended to other firms had it
not been checked. Other eases could be cited to
show the necessity of our union, but we think no
further proof is required, and that it will be a sorry
day for us when we refuse to unite together for
our common good; when we shall -be so careless 9f
our interests as to leave others to do for us what
we ought to do for ourselves; when we Shall exist
only as individuals, and thereby become reducedto
the weakness of a unit, when by combination we
can be strong."

articles.title: CHESTER ENGINEERS AND THE CRIgINAL LAW AMEND-
articles.text:
THE CHESTER ENGINEERS
AND THE CRIgINAL LAW AMEND-

"'TENT ACT.

On Saturday last Mr. H. C. Raikos, M.P., • re-
ceived a deputation from the Chester Branch of the
Atottigitiuded Society of Engineers, consitting of
Messrs. T. Jones,, W. Williams, S. Monk,G:
quhoun, H. Parker, G. Worsloy,H, Sharpies, and
D. Arthur. ,

Mr. T. Jones, after introducing tho deputation,
stated that tho satiety tvhielt thoy represented
numbered upwards of 403000 members, and had
been in existence for nineteen years; that their
present funds amounted to about Z170,f4)0
that they had distributed since their formation be-
tween X.410030tY0 and 4900;00Q in sick end benefit
grants tind superannuation aliowatree.

Mr. W. "Williams then said that the deputation
bad waited upon Mr. Raikes, not only as the re-
presentatives of the Engineers' Society but also
of trades unions generally, and of all working
men. Their object now was to protest against the
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1871, which they
regarded as a piece of class legislation. They
were not a political society, their members be-
longed to various shades of politics, but in this
they were united, that they would combine for the
defence of their labour. Their object was the
protection of trades unionism as legitimately car-
ried out. The speaker then entered upon a short
history of the legal enactments affecting trades
unionism, and stated that what the working men
wanted was the repeal or amendment of this arbi-
trary Act.
Mr. Raikes, M.P., then replied at length to the
deputation, stating that he had not been able to
awe with some of the provisions of the Act and
had not voted in its favour. At the same time it
was a question of very serious importance, and
must be looked at from different aspects. He was
not an employer himself, and therefore could have
no bias against the men. The aspect in which
the question presented itself to him personally was
from the consumer's point of view ; but that would
not prevent him from looking at it from their
point too. He reminded the deputation that the
party to which he belonged had been mainly in-
strumental in carrying the Acts which most bene-
fited the working classes, especially the Factory
Acts, which shortened the hours of labour, and
provided that the bodily health of the workers
should not be injured. He was very glad to have
beard the views of the working men so ably and
dispassionately stated, and should have great plea-
sure in carefully considering any amendments
which might be submitted to him. He invited the
deputation to submit to him any scheme which
they might agree upon, and promised that he would
give his support to such an amendment of the
law as might seem best calculated to do away with
the necessity of strikes.

been raised socially and politically, he thought

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS'
articles.text:
THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS'

UNION.

The hi-monthly meeting of the Executive Com-
mittee of the National Agricultural Labourers'
Union was held on Monday at the offices, For-
field-place, Leamington. Mr. Joseph Arch, the
president, occupied the chair. There were present
Messrs. Haynes, Harris, Parker, Jordan, Russell,
Prickett, Blackwell, Wright, Collins, Campbell,

district on the 27th inst. and that of Huntingdon

Leamington meeting,
Numerous applications were received from de-
crepid and old men, who were too old to migrate,
asking for assistance, in consequence of having
been refused relief from the poor rates, on the
ground that they were members of the Labourers'
Union. It was decided that renewed application
should be made for relief, and if refuse], then that
steps should be taken to test the right of the
Guaraians to refuse relief under sueh circum-
stances.

A. resolution was adopted, expressing the
gratitude of the Union to the friends of the
movement in London, for the sympathy evinced
at the Exeter Hall meeting, and expressing much
regret that Mr. Bradlaugh took advantage of the
opportunity to bring forward his own peculiar
views, to the injury of the cause of the agricul-
tural labourer.

It was decided to forward £lOO to labourers in
Dorset, to assist the men to migrate; and to
forward £6O to Essex, to assist the men locked
out in that county. The secretary was directed to
frame rules for the projected Union Sick and
Benefit Society, and to submit a draft at the next
meeting.
The Committee laid down this principle as to
emigration.

That, where a Government advances passage
money, to be repaid in instalments by the emi-
grant, the Union will not afford any assistance.
Mr. Arch, it was arranged, should visit Bud-
dersfield, and then proceed to Norfolk, where Mr.
Taylor will renew his labours at once; that Mr.
Jordan should visit Warwickshire, Mr. Russell,
Worcestershire, with Mr. Haynes; that Mr.
Harris ehould continue his labours in Northamp-
tonshire, and Mr. Allington go to Somerset.
The necessity of taking steps in favour of an
ssztension of the franchise to working men was
discussed, and it was decided to submit to the

Union meetings petitions in favour of assimilating
the franchise in counties to that in boroughs, and
also urging the House of Commons to consider next
sessiop the important question of the redistribu-
tion of seats.

articles.title: CONFERENCE OF IRONMASTERS
articles.text:
CONFERENCE OF IRONMASTERS

AND IRONWORKERS.

An important Conference of ironmastera and
ironworkers was held on Monday at Wolver-
hampton. _

The masters were represented by Mr. George
Barker, chairman of the Ironmasters' Association ;
the Agent of the Earl of Dudley, Mr. William
Orme Foster, and eight others.
The men were represented by the 12 iron-
workers who are the Operatives' Conciliation Com-
mittee.

The business had especial reference to the wages
scale after this year. The masters complained
that the men had broken the agreement on which
wages had been based in the past six months, and
they thought the action of the men in South Staf-
fordshire and the North of England, in breaking
agreements, discouraged the masters in respect of
conciliation and arbitration; but they wished to
give the principle a further trial. The men replied
that when they were as well organized as the
masters they should be able to keep their engage-
ments as faithfully, and urged that the masters
must share the responsibility in respect of the
South Staffordshire complaint. As to the future,
they expected that the wages in the next six months
would be based upon the average price of bars in
the past six months, and the Is. per ton bonus.
For certain modifications in their favour, Stafford-
shire and tho North of England would memorialise
about June. The masters held that there was no
agreement as to the future, adducing tho short-
hand writer's notes in proof, but they offered to
continue for three or four months longer to pay as
now, 12s. Gd. per ton for puddling, to afford time
for the Operatives' Committee to consult their
constituents.

The Conference was adjourned for a week.
The settling of the question before Christmas was
mutually desired.

articles.title: BUILDING TRADES AT
articles.text:
THE BUILDING TRADES AT

REDDITCH.

At Redditch, a meeting of workmen employed
in the various departments of the building trade
was held on Thursday evening, in the, large room
of the Fox and Goose Hotel. Mr. James Badger,
carpenter, was elected to the chair. In explaining
the object of the meeting, he observed that it was
to consider the means to be adopted for the purpose
of altering their present condition, viz., to bring
it up to its former standard,. because, in conse-
quence of the increased price of provisions, &c.,
they were not now in as good a position as in pre-
vious years, when they received lower wages.
Mr. Geoege Hinne, carpenter, moved the follow-
ing resolution
That a notice be served upon the master
builders from the carpenters, soliciting that the
wages now paid shall be advanced from 51d. to
GO. per hour, with the same advance on all over-
time.

Mr. A. Field seconded the proposition, and it
was unanimcusly carried.
On behalf of the bricklayers present, Mr. J.
Guise proposed a resolution similar to that of the
carpenters, stating the same amounts, and the
same rate of increase. This was seconded by Mr.
A. Stylor, and carried.
The masons' labourers also had a proposition to
make, which was put into the hands of Mr. Wm.
Shoroy, who observed that at present they were
paid by the week, but had thought it best they
should be put upon the hour system, and work the
same hours as the bricklayers. He would there-
fore propose—
That a notice be served upon the masters, re-
questing them to put the bricklayers' labourers
upon the hour system, and that their wages be fixed
at 40. per hour.

This was seconded by Mr. J. Hawthorne, and
passed.

Some discussion followed respecting the time at
which the notices should be served, the chairman
and several others agreeing that they should each
be serve(' on the same day; but it was ultimately
decided that the rules of the respective lodges he
adhered to, which provided that notices from the
carpenters be served on or before the Dith of
December in any year, and that those from the
bricklayers and labourers be served on the Ist day

THE SUNDAY REST ASSOCIATION.

On Saturday morning a numerously attended
deputation waited by appointment upon the
Archbishop of Canterbury r.t Lambeth Palace
for the purpose of explaining the recent action
of the society in promoting the voluntary
closing of shops on Sunday, and to solicit his
Grace's co-operation in carrying out several
suggestions which had been discussed at the
recent meetings of the committee in Turther-
ance of this object. Amongst the gentlemen
forming the deputation were Mr. Samuel
Morley, M.P., Mr. Charles Reed, M.P., Mr.
M'Arthur, M.P., the Rev. R. J. Simpson, Revs.
Tugwell, Tyler, Gritton, M'Culloch, G. M.
Murphy, Mr. Wilson, Mr. John Palmer, the
Rev. Alfred Jones, the secretary, and other
friends of the association. _ _ _ _

Mr. Samuel Morley introduced the deputa-
tion to the Archbishop, and briefly stated the
purpose for which they had requested an in-
terview with his grace. The Sunday Rest
Association had been engaged for some time
past in obtaining, by arrangement, tho volun-
tary closing of shops on the Lord's Day.
Instead of threatening them with the penalties
of the law, they had shown them the social
and other Avantages which the observance of
the Lord's Day would confer upon a district,
and they had reason to believe that this course
had been attended with considerable success.
But in order to effect a still further improve-
ment, they were present that morning to
solicit his grace's co-operation in several fresh
efforts which had been discussed, and which,
if carried out with energy, would, he (Mr.
Morley) believed, give a considerable impetus
to the movement. They proposed, in the
first place, to hold a meeting in Lambeth—the
Lambeth Baths in the New-cut had been sug-
gested—to which the tradesmen and coster-
mongers would be invited, and over that
meeting they would be thankful if his grace
would do them the honour to preside. The
second suggestion was to ask the archbishop
in *company with a few friends of the asso-
ciation, to walk through the New-cut on some
Sunday morning, and on the spot to address a
few words to the people upon the subject of
Sunday trading. A third proposition was,
that in order to direct public opinion to this
evil, clergymen and ministers of all denomina-
tions should be invited to set apart a Sunday
early in the new year. for the purpose of bring-
ing the subject specially before their respective
congregations. Public opinion would thus, it
was hoped, be brought to bear upon the subject.
The association wished to plead with the
people who are at present desecrating the
Sabbath ; and, in the carrying out of each of
the suggestions, he (Mr. Morley) believed that
the personal co-operation of the Archbishop
would be invaluable.

The Rev. It. J. Simpson, as the author of
the resolution advocating the preaching of
sermons on this subject in our churches and
chapels on a special Sunday, bore testimony
to the importance of the movement, and of the
benefits that would result from a united effort.

The Rev. Mr. Tyler, of Spitaltields, believed
that the question of the proper observance of
Sunday was never in a more hopeful condition
than at the present time.
The Rev. Alfred Jones, the indefatigable
secretary of the association, referred to the
various measures which had been initiated for
the purpose of obtaining the closing of shops
on Sunday in Lambeth.
Mr. Mackness, a tradesman in the New-cut,
remarked that it was only a small minority
that opposed the general closing of shops on
Sundays in the neighbourhood of the New-cut,
and he believed that nothing short of the en-
forcement of the law would remedy the evil.
Mr, John Palmer detailed his experience in
one of the districts where the operations of the
association had recently been carried on. This
district included the streets south of the New-
cut, and extended west vard as far as the
Archbishop's palace. There were in all 619
shops, 248 of which were open on Sunday.
Believing that the best way of grappling with
the evil was by taking it in detail, Lambeth-
walk had been thoroughly canvassed, ani up
to the present time with the following results.
There were 193 shops, of which 103 were Open
on Sunday. Of these 23 were public-houses,
chemists, &c., already dealt with by act of
parliament, 7 of the proprietors had not been
seen, 27 had refused to consent to the request
of the association, but 44 had not only promised
to discontinue Sunday trading, but most of
them had expressed a hope that the closing
would be general. Out of the 44 twenty had
signed a book consenting to abandon Sunday
trading on the first Sunday in the new year.
The Rev. (I-. M. Murphy bore testimony to
the improved character of the New-cut, a dis-
trict in which he had worked for many years,
and he believed that the proposed meeting
would be most beneficial.
The Archbishop of Canterbury, in reply,
expressed the pleasure it gave him to meet the
gentlemen present, who were engaged in a
work which had his hearty sympathy. Ho
should be glad to co-operate with them, and
would do all he could to further the object
they had in view. it a convenient day could
be fixed he would be happy to preside at the
' meeting, although his health prevented him
from attending evening meetings. He would,

however, be glad to meet them at the Lambeth
Baths, and also to accompany them through
the New-cat, as had been suggested.
A conversation then took place as to the
date of the meeting. After some discussion it
was ultimately agreed that the meeting at the
Lambeth Baths should be held on Wednesday,
the sth of February, 1873, at eight o'clock,
under the presidency of the Archbishop;
Sunday, the 9th of February, was fixed as the
date for the " walk through the New-cut;
aud February 16th (subject to the sanction of
the Bishops of London, Winchester, and
Rochester) for the special sermons. •

articles.title: MINISTERS OF RELIGION AND WORKING MEN. To the Editor of the BEE HIVE.
articles.text:
MINISTERS OF RELIGION AND
WORKING MEN.
To the Editor of the BEE HIVE.

Sin,—Being a subscriber and admirer of
your valuable paper, and also a working man,
am, as, indeed, every working man should
be, a friend of progress, and am sensible of the
fact that a great deal of hostility exists, and
bitter feelings are engendered by, speeches and
sermons delivered by bishops and other clergy-
men; also after dinner speeches by aristocrats
and landowners. Generally, for my own part,
Ido not think it comes with good grace from
either party, for 1 do believe that the working
men of England can manage their own affairs,
also regulate their wages without consulting
the bishops or aristocrats of this country. But
theu the clergy are not all alike—" God forbid
they should." I have sent you the following
letter from last week's Taimeorth Herald,
which I should like you to publish next week,
by the Rev. Brooke Lambert, the vicar of this
borough. He is a true friend of the working
class and agricultural labourer, but of course
not in much favour with employers. The
working men here have got him on their side,
and intend to keep him if p9sslble.—l am,
dear sir, yours truly,
Aldersgate-stroot, Tamworth.

Mos. FILDES.

Sin,—A piece of poetry appeared in your last
impression in which in some lines prettily fashioned
after the model of a celebrated soliloquy in Hamlet,
the writer discussed the question of strikes, and
imagined that some childless man had, in imputing
heroism to those who joined a Union, forgotten the
wives and children of the hero. •
Now this touches a very intimate friend of mine,
whom I meet, say once a day—in tho looking
glass. I wish therefore to say a word on the sub-
ject of strikes.
And first I think the writer errs in fact, in im-
puting great suffering, of necessity, to the wives
and children of those who strike. There may be
exceptional cases; but as a rule, belonging to a
Union entitles the man to a bare subsistence for
his wife and children. He does not depend on the
funds of his Own Trades Union, which in a country
place might be very small, but on the collections
and contributions made for him in other Trades
Unions; and by Means of these he is either sup-
ported at home, or transferred to some other place
where he can get better work. The hardship falls
largely on himself if he belongs to a skilled trade.
In the agricultural labourer's case however, it
would be almost impossible for the Union to fix
an allowance smaller than his ordinary wages.
That is a question of fad on which I am at issue
with the writer.
But, even supposing these are not exceptional
cases whichrhave stirred the writer, but that they
are the rule—that as ail& the wives and children
of the men on strike went on very short commons,
for I have never seen a case of starvation reported
—would that be it just argument for a man to re-
fuse to incur, in the interests of the trade to which
he below, these risks?
The writer of the lines makes my friend call
these men heroes. He would I know endorse the
word—but the very word hero implies the sacri-
fice not only of his own life, but of the comfort of
others. The word is usually applied to fighting
men. Supposing it was necessary to procure
volunteers for a war against the French, the Ger-
man, or any other foes old or new, would it be an
argument to which men ought to listen that if
they joined the band of heroes, they would leave
their wives and children unprotected, and unsup-
ported? The writer would probably answer—No !
the good of their country desires the terrible uteri-
`

It is just because I believe the good of the class
to which they belong .is quite as valuable as the
good of the country at large,—for the whole coun-
try cannot be prosperous, if one class in it is
underpaid or works for wages not sufficient to
provide a maintenance in old age, or fixed at a rate
less than the profits of the trade allow (for we
must concede that the labour invested is a part of
the capital of the concern since without labour
capital would be useless)—that whilst I think
strikes useful, I agree with my friend that those
who incur hardships in their prosecution are
heroes.
And now let us just see what strikes are. They
are in point of fact the means by which men test
what capital can afford to give them.* The con-
tention of capitalists all through has been that they
paid as much as they could afford, and that if they
paid more trade would become unremunerative.
Nevertheless it is an incontestable fact that wages
have risen, and the manufacturers have not been
ruined. Why? Necessity in this, as other cases,
has been the mother of invention. New machines
have been constructed, economies have been insti-
tuted, which have not only produced the same
articles at less cost, but have further so stimulated
production that, with an increase of wages, there
has been an increase of manufacture. Without
strikes, that is the refusal to work at a low wage,
men could never have found out what was the
proper value of their work.
But strikes are a clumsy method of coming at
this result, a method which I hope that another
century will make as obsolete as the handlooms,
and other clumsy machinery of the past. Arbitra-
tion is fast superseding strikes, and by and by it
may be hoped that some method of estimating the

ratio between the value of the capital in lab our,
and the capital in money will be instituted.
There is one argument against strikes often
used, to which I should like to reply. It is said
that men don't know bow to use the money they
have already got, and that therefore it is absurd to
give them more. When a child first 'meta a knife,
it usually cuts its fingers with it. Familiarity
with the knife enables It to use it for good, and not
for bad. Ido not think that the expenditure of
the working classes contrasts so very unfavourably
with that of many of our rich folk who ruin them-
selves on race courses, and in millinery. But I
believe a large amount of the evil arises from un-
familiarity with the use of money, and is an in-
heritance of past ages of misery. There were times,
be it said to the shame of England, when the
labouring man had no amusement but the public
house. He could not read, how else could he
employ his leisure. Hence drink became the
traditional amusement, and anyone who knows
how customs linger long after their meaning is
gone by, can understand why the first thing a man
does with a pocketful of money is to stand treat
with it all round. It may take a century yet to
do away with this habit, which once indulged in
becomes the parent of numberless other ills. Let
men have comfortable homes, let them have some
enjoyments for their leisure hour, let them not
be so worn down with 12 hours toil (I speak of
agricultural labourers) as to make drink, or sleep
the only possible amusement for any but very
strong, or a very self-contained man; and as man
is man, and not beast by nature, he will rise above
his temptations become accessible to the claims of
religion, and of home duties, and spend his money
well.—Yours, eze.,
BROOKE LAMBERT.
• I speak of the majority of capitalists—l
know some, and some here who have advanced
wages on a temperate representation from their
men.

articles.text:
FOREST RIGHTS.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
have the honour to request you will
insert in your valuable journal the following
letter just received. The reliable statement it
contains should at once set at rest the doubts
which have assumed some consistency since
the speech of the Chancellor of the Exchequer
at Glasgow, as to the existence of deer
within the Forest of.Epping.—l am, sir, your
obedient servant,
W. C. SMITH, Hon. Sec. Forest Fund.
Rose Cottage, Forest Gate, E.

"Chesnut House Forest Gate, E.
December 14th, 1872.
DEAR SIR,—It will be gratifying toyou and
the gentlemen associated with you in your
efforts to preserve Epping Forest for the
people, to hear the following incident which
has happened to me this morning. While
driving in company with Mr. Baker, late of
the "Eagle and Child," Forest Gate, to witness
the meet at Coopersale, and when about 400
yardi from the " Wake Arms," Epping-place,
we were startled by the appearance of three
fine deer crossing the road about 200 yards in
front of us. The weather being very hazy
will account, I presume, for their close proxt
mity. Upon making inquiries in the village,
we were informed a herd of six or eight mem-
bers, in good condition, have been frequently
seen of late.—l am, dear sir, yours truly,
WILLIAM SAMPSON.

THE LETTER CARRIERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sta,—Will you allow me through the
medium of your paper to convey to the post-
men that an influential member of Parliament
has consented to more in the House of Com-
mons early next Session for a 'copy of the
petitions presented by the minor establishment
of the Post-office, and will also ask some im-
portant questions respecting them; he will
also move for a return of salaries increased in
the major establishment, the amount, the back
pay received, the previous amount of salary
received, and for what given. It has been
necessary to get a member of Parliament to
take up our cause, owing to the treatment our
petitions have Met with at the
.hands of our
superiors in the major establishment, who
have, in every instance, received a large
addition to their already large salaries, as well
as received very large sums as back pay. If
the already greatly overpaid and under-
worked of the major establishment needed an
increase, surely the overworked and much
less underpaid need some increase. Large
public meetings are about to be held, and fresh
petitions sent direct to the Government.
Several influential persons have consented to
take part in them, and lay before the public
the facts connected with our case. It has
been said that the postmen are the only body
who have not been increased in pay. Why,
sir, is this? It is, because, we do not strike.
.If so, we shall never get it; for we do not in-
tend to strike; we will live on bread and
W iter first.—Your obedient servant,
()NE OF Tun LETTER CABUIERfe COMMITTEE.

SLANDER AND THE ATIIINA.SIAN

CREED.
To the Editor of the BE HrvE.
Sin,—To be acoused falsely by men servilely
professing to be friends of having been guilty
of an offence which only the bitterest enemies
would falsely accuse a man of, or wish that a
man might be accused of, viz., of exalting

himself to be either God or equal with God,
this is
"The most unpardonable offence."
And it is also the height of impudence when
these professed friends, without shame, and
.with the boldest effrontery, use the Very
name of the accused man as a God, in order to
claim for themselves infallible ani divine
authority to damn and to excommunicate all
who refuse either to worship this man as God,
or to receive these fallible and sinful men, his
professed friends, as infallible and divine
priests of God, notwithstanding the fact that
they are even confessedly inoapable of either
understanding God or even proving the exist-
ence of God.
And the modern priest and pharisee is
guilty of this offence when he asserts that
Jesus of Nazareth is either God or equal with
God, because even the accusation of the ancient
proud priests, written on the Cross itself in
Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, does not charge
Jesus with making himself either God or equal
with God, but only with making himself
"the King of the Jews."—John xix 19.
Then is it not the most unpardonable offence
for modern priests and pharisees to require the
people to worship as God, or as equal with
God, the man Jesus who so nobly devoted his
life to deliver and save the World from a bar-
barous and inhuman religion, in order to bring
men to worship, not himself, but his Father
and our Father, his God and our God (John
xx., 17), after the manner of his own example,
viz., with deeds of love and mercy, instead of
with the blood either of bulls and goats, or of
human beings either sinful or righteous, and
still less with the empty profession of am-
biguous and irreoonoileable creeds?
T. G. HEADLEY.
Petersham, S.W.

THE MEETING AT E ZETER, HILL AND
TUE TIMES.
To the Editor of the BEE HIVE:
SIR,—The leader in the Times of the 11th
says, "To keep down the supply of farm labour
is the only way of improving the farm
labourers' condition. This is what Canon
Girdlestone, whose absence was conspicuous
last night, has been doing, and he deserves all
honour for it. What said Goldsmith in his
beautiful poem the "Disturbed Village ? "

"111 fares the land to hastening ills a prey,
Where wealth accumulates and men decay,
Princes and kings may flourish or may fade
A breath can make them as a 'breath has made;
But a bold peasantry, the countrie's pride,
When once destroy'd can never be supplied."

•
This, with all their good intentions, is
sounder doctrine than that of the 2'intes or
Canon Gridlestone's. Again' we see in this
day's Times, copied from the Pall Mall
Gazette, a paragraph showing a fearful state
of things among the emigrants sent to some
part of the Brazilian Empire in May last.
Their letters are of a painfully interesting
character. "They have used us very badly,"
says one. " We have not tasted broad since
we have been here. . . We live together
like pigs; in worse than pigsties; and we
shall soon all
,he pined to death here. We
would not have come hero for all the world
if we had known. . . There are 114 out

here with us, and we have all petitioned the
Emperor to come back. There have five died.
in. three weeks." Another complains:—" They
have deceived us very much. You may expect
me back as soon as I have the money, and be
sure and tell my brother George not to come
out here, for it's no good, for they never ful-
filled their promises. We have not found
anything .here that they have said. The
houses are not so good as in England. We
have nothing to eat but black beans and rice.
There is no bread here. We have no bed to
lie upon but the - cold ground. I have not
undressed but three times since I left old
England."
Now, we wish to point out the fact that
these three United Kingdoms is capable of
sustaining within its area, in perfect happituise
and employment, with ample means of feeding,
with all the oomforts and luxuries the world
can produce' 100,000,000 of inhabitants, and
with more harmony than at present exists
with only 30,000,000 in round numbers, the
first condition being the policy of the "Free
Breakfast Table," and yet the Times can only
reiterate that, "All other schemes are but
temporary expedients, if not worse," whilst
it has not the moral courage to accept our
challenge to discuss in its columns the question
of the "Free Breakfast Table. And the Pall
Mall Gazette says, "It would be interesting
to know who is responsible for the sufferings
these unfortunate emigrants have endured,"
not perceiving the "beam in its own eye,"
which prevents it seeing the vast importance
which attaches to , the question of entire Free
Trade as regards the profitable employment of
the people.—Yours,
Dec. 17th.

T. Boaas.
