articles.text:
LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

On Wednesday the weekly meeting of this
Board was held at Guildhall—Alderman
Lawrence in 'the chair.
The Finance Committee reported that they
had resolved that the £lOO, which was pre-
sented to them, through Lady Burdett Coutts,
by the Ladies' Committee of the Royal Society
for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals,
should not be expended before Miohaelmas,
1873. They considered it advisable that any
amount that can be obtained as interest should.
be added to the principal, thus increasing the
sum to be distributed as prizes amongst pupil
teachers and children. The same committee
had received a letter from Messrs. Yates and
Alexander, the printers to the Board, drawiag
attention to the large increase in the wages
paid to their workmen, and of the rise in the
price of paper, and asking that their contract
with the Board of the sth of April, 1871, may
be amended by a reduction of 10 per cent.
upon the rate of discount to be allowed by
them on the contract prices, and it was tocom-
mended that the proposed reduction be sanc-
tioned. -
The recommendations of the committee were
approved of.
Mr Freeman brought up a report from the
Finance Committee, which stated that the
Education Department had recommended the
Public Works Loan Commissioners to advance
to the Board £45,268 to meet expenditure for
purchase of sites, &., for certain schools, being
part of the second loan of £150,000 agreed to
be advanced by the Commissioners to the Board.
£34,127 had been expended upon this account.
The committee recommended that the common
seal of the Board be affixed to the mortgage of
the rates for £34,127 and further advances,
not exceeding therewith £/5,208, and to an
order authorising the certificate for the said
£34,127, to be delivered to the Governors and
Company of the Bank of England, the
treasurers of the Board.

The Statistical Committee presented a long
report respecting the complaints which have
been made with regard to the establishment of
Board Schools in Bath-street, City-road.
After carefully considering all the questions
and interests involved, the committee came to,
the conclusion that no valid objections have
been made to the course of !lotion already de-
cided upon by the Board, and that there will
be ample room in Blocks W, X, and A D for
all the schools proposed. But they reoom-
mended that, without abandoning the schools
now temporarily held in Bath-street, no steps
should be taken to provide a permanent site in
until the schools in Central-street and Charles-
street shall have been built and tilled.

This report gavo rise to a prolonged dis-
cussion, of a similar character to the many
oth6r discussions on the same subject which
have taken place. Ultimately, the recom-
mendation of the committee was approved of,
with tha addition of words assuring the con-
tinuance of the existing Bath-street school in
the meantime.

The adjourned debate on the Rey. Dr.
Barry's motion respecting the readings of the
Bible in Board Schools, and the instruction
which should follow, was further postponed
till the 15th January next, when it is to take
precedence of other business.

After disposing of the other items on the
paper, the Board adjourned over Christmas,
till Wednesday, the Bth January, 1873.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

tie Japanese Ambassador, and suite of
twenty-three gentlemen in attendance on his
Excellency, arrived in Dover on Monday
morning by the London, Chatham, and Dover
boat train from Victoria Station, accompanied
by General Alexander, of the R.M.H. His
Excellency was received at the Admiralty Pier
by Captain Bruce, R.N., Colonel Macdonald,
and staff, and Mr. Forbes, manager of the
London, Chatham, and Dover Railway. A.
salute was fired from the Caste. His Excel-
lency left in the special packet Wave, Captain
Bennett, for Calais.

On Saturday afternoon, at Ribstone-park,
the seat of Mr. J. D. Dent, M.P., whilst that
gentleman was out shooting with some friends,
one of the party accidentally shot Mr. Dundas,
M.P., nephew tá the Earl of &Hand, in one of
his. eyes. The best medical aid was called
and Mr. Dundas was removed to Swaroliffe-
hall, the seat of Mr. Greenwood, where the hon.
gentleman is staying.

At Exeter, Tannaker Buckarosa, manager
of a Japanese troupe which appeared at several
places in the metropolis a short time since,
was fiaed £lO, for ill-treating a child four and
a half years old. It was proved that be had
severely chatised the child, 'kept it on bread
and water all day in a dark cupboard, having
buckled its hands over the head to prevent him
from going to sleep.

Mr. Edmund Yates lectured twice recently
before crowded houses in Philadelphia at the
Academy of Music, and In Washington before
a large audience at Lincoln Hall, which in-
cluded the British 4linister, Sir Edward
Thornton, and his suite, as. well as Secretaries
Boutwell and Robeson. On the 2nd instant
Mr. Yates was announced to appear before a
metropolitan audience at Steinway Hall, with
a lecture on the "British Parliament," after
which he was to leave the city for a prolonged
tour of two months, every night of which was
engaged.

The Russian Official Gazette announces
that a diploma of honour has been conferred
upon Baron Liebig, for the application of his
knowledge of theoretical chemistry to practical
I urposes,

On Monday, the Prince of Wales, as Presi-
dent of the bociety of Arts, presented to Mr.
Henry Bessemer the Albert Gold Medal, for his
eminent services in developing the manu-
facture orsteel.

A numerous deputation, representing the
Royal Geographical Society, the British
Association, Anthropological Institute, and
other scientific bodies, on Monday waited upon
the Chancellor of the Exchequer and Mr.
Goscheu, to ask for a renewal of the work of
Arctic exploration under the aid and direction
of the Government, It was stated that two
steam whalers would be ample for the purpose
contemplated, and that a contribution of 120
men would be sufficient. The ships would be
provisioned for three years, and, according to
Captain Shoran'. Osborn, about three summers
anti two winters would have to be passed in
the Arctic, regions. The Chancellor of the Ex-
Oleg uer promised to consider, with his colleague,
all that had been urged, and to read over the
papers and documents which had, been left
with them for oonsideratien.

President Grant, in referring to the San
ban Award in his Message observed—" It
io my grateful duty to acknowledge the prompt
spontaneous action of her Majesty's Govern-
ment in , giving effect to the award. In
azitioipation of any request from this Govern-
Ment, and before the, reception in the United
States of the award signed by the Emperor,
her Majesty had given instructions for the
removal of her troops which had been
stationed there, and for the cessation of all
exercise or claim of jurisdiction, so as to leave
the United States in exclusive possession of
the lately disputed territory."

On Monday morning a passenger train ran
into two other trains standing before it on the
Lancashire and Yorkshire line, near Lowmoor,
and several people, were shaken and bruised,
but not injured to any serious extent.

Admiral Sir John Lyons, brother of the
late Admiral Lord Lyons, died on Monday, at
his residence at Worthing, Admiral Lyons
served on board the Victory, Nelson's flagship,
at Trafalgar.

- In concluding the inqury into the mys-
terious death of the woman who was found in
a tunnel of the Underground Railway near
Charing-arose, the jury returned an open
verdict, the evidence not being oonclusive as
to how the fatal injuries were caused.

Albert Drayton, a brave man, who did con-
spicuoua service in saving life when the Royal
Adelaide was lost, has just died from the
effects of the over-exertion and exposure on
the beach.

At the Liverpool Assizes on Monday Mr.
Justice Mellor sentenced to death a man and
woman who had been convicted of murder.
One of the condemned is Catherine Hanlon, a
hawker, who recently stabbed a boy in the
stomach, inflicting such a wound as to cause
death in a few days; the other is Richard
Spencer, a fishmonger, who some time ago,
shot a woman with whom he had been living
for fifteen years. He also shot himself, and
has only just recovered from the wounds.

On Monday the Bishop of Manchester pre-
sided at a meeting in aid of the funds of the
Shipwrecked Fishermen and Mariners' Royal
Benevolent Society at Manchester, and made
an eloquent appeal on behalf of the institu-
tion. In the course of his speech he said that
competition in commerce had become so keen
that very often cargoes wero put into unsea
worthy vessels. Our coast, too, he was
ashamed to say, was infamously ill-lighted,
as compared with the coast of France.

One of the clerks in Devonport Dockyard,
on the permanent staff, and in receipt of over
£3OO per annum, is under suspension by the
Admiral - Superintendent, pending further
proceedings. His account had been found
deficient to the extent of £43. He would be
entitled to nearly £2OO per annum super-
annuation on retirement.

No intelligence having been received of the
large new screw steamship Counsellor, of
North Shields, now about a fortnight overdue,
little doubt is entertained that she is lost.
The Counsellor had a crew of twenty hands.
Great anxiety is being evinced for the safety
of the screw steam-ship ChiHingham Castle,
belonging to Newcastle which is also much
overdue, She had a crew of twenty-two in
number.

Fourteen of the rioters at the Stockton
Amnesty meeting on Sunday were brought
before the magistrates on Monday. Of these
six were sentenced to three months' hard
labour, three to two months, and one to one
month. At South Stockton, several persons
charged with riotous conduct were fined 40s.
and costs. Defendants were nearly all Irish.

Before the Stipendiary Magistrate at Leeds,
on Monday, Thomas by, a butcher, for having
sold the carcase of a diseased sheep, supposed
to have been bitten by a mad dog, was sent to
prison for three months. The defendant was
astounded at the sentence, and wished to
address the Stipendiary; who, however, re-
fused to hear him.

Proceedings of a very stormy character took
place at the adjourned meeting of the National
Union for the Suppression of Intemperance, at
Liverpool, on Monday, called to hear the
reply of Dr. Garrett, chairman of the executive,
to the charges of extravagance, and unwarrant-
able publication of Liverpool names on the
committee. These accusations were made by
Mr. W. S. Caine, and Dr. Garrett in his
answer contended that a clause in the society's
circulars, making subscribers of a certain sum
eligible as vice-presidents, was a sufficient
warranty for the publication of subscribers'
names, either as vice-presidents, or committee-
men, since vice-presidents were ex (lido mem-
bers of committee. After an excited discussion,
it was resolved "That this meeting having
heard the explanations of Dr. Garrett, has no
confidence in the National Union for the Sup-
pression of Intemperance."

'At last the hearing of evidence and argu-
ments in the great financial suit of Parker v.
Lewis and others has been brought to a close
—the Solicitor-General haying on Tuesday re-
plied for the plaintiff on the whole ease. The
Vice-Chancellor said that the importance and
the complexity of the case required him to
postpoqe judgment until January; and paid a
tribute to the skill and ability with which the
suit had been conducted.

In the Court if Queen's Bench, an action for
libel was brought by the General South Ameri-
can Company, (Limited), who sought to re-
cover damages from Dr. Buzo, an agent or
commissioner of the Peruvian Government,
sent to this country to examine into certain
frauds connected with the importation of guano
hither. The defendant had, it seems, in a
letter, amused the company of participation in
the frauds, but on a' full and free withdrawal
of the imputations, made by the Attorney-
General on his behalf, the Court permitted an
arrangement to be made, the Lord Chief
Justice describing the termination of the ease
as " honourable to both sides."

Tho Civil Tribunal of the Soine has rejected
the opposition of the Princess of Moskowa to
the marriage of her daughter, the Duchess de
Persigny with M. Letnoinne.

A fire occurred on Monday night on the
premises of Mr. Mader, Fleet-street, Torquay.
A servant girl was trimming a benzoline lamp,
when it uphet, setting fire to the house, which
was destroyed in two hours. Three men were
injured, but no lives were lost.— The damage
is estimated at £3,000.

On the oecasion of the annual market in
Berneck, St. Gall (says the Swiss Times), an
innkeeper while carving a Californian ham,
came upon a nugget of gold of the size of a
walnut. The lucky find, weighing 151
grammes, proved to be of the finest. gold. It
is well known that various hard substances
find their way into pigs' stomachs, but the
discovery of a nugget of pare gold in this way
may be esteemed a novelty.

Owing to insufficiency in the deliveries of
iron at Chatham Dockyard of late the two iron
composite gun-vessels now building there—
the Zephyr and the Arid—will not be launched
so soon as was expected. •

Alfred Mack, 17, labourer, was indicted at
the Middlesex Sessions for a robbery with
violence on Harry Clifton, and stealing from
him, a watch and chain. The prosecutor was
passino. along Bethnal-green-road on the even-
ing of 29th November, when he observed
' three men one of whom ;tole his watch and
chain and ran off. The prosecutor pursued
him and the prisoner took up a large stone
andAhrew it at him. A policeman came up,
and the prisoner ran into his arms. The jury
found him guilty, and he was sentenced to
twelve months' imprisonment.

At tho Gravesend petty sessions on Monday
a youth attended and asked if there would be
any objection to the drum and fife band being
out until about midnight on Christmas Eve.
The Mayo:, whose name is Wates, said that
all the public-houses would be closed at
eleven o'clock, and consequently the magis-
trates could not grant the application. •

Charles Watson, who described himself as a
member of the Royal College of Surgeons,
pleaded guilty, at the Middlesex Sessions on
Tuesday, to an indictment charging him with
publishing an obscene book. Mr. Commis-
sioner Kerr said the defendant was one of
these against whom the public, and especially
weak-minded young men, must be protected.
He required him to enter.into his own recog-
nisances for £l,OOO to come up for judgment
if called upon, remarking that it another case of
this kind were brought before him a severe
punishment would be inflicted.

A member of the sect known as the
" Shakers " on Monday waited upon Mr.
Woolryoll at the Westminster Police-court,
and complained that on Sunday evenings the
worshippers who met in College-street, Chelsea,
were annoyed by a number of persons who
pelted them with bags of lime and other
missiles. The applicant gave some informa-
tion respecting the peculiar form of worship
and the mode of ministration adopted by the
religious body of which he is a member; and
from what he stated, Mr. Woolryoh suggested
that the blow which the man said he received
in the street might have been dealt by an en-
thusiastio member of the congregation. He,
however, directed the police to give the
matter their attention.

Herr Ka.mpschulte, Professor of History at
Bonn, who died, the other day, has been interred
with all the ceremonials of the Roman Catholic
Church, although to his last moment he was a
strong opponent of the dogma of Papal Infalli-
bility. The service was performed by his
friend and colleague, the cure, Reusch,
Professor of Theology in, the same univer-
sity.

The Dublin Evening Post says that one of
the most popular members of the movement
has "made the candid statement that in Mun-
ster the Home Rule Association was unknown,
but .that a sentiment in favour of Home Rule
and Nationality was spreading among the
people." .

A Daily News telegram from Rome says that
in consequence of the vote of the Private Com-
mittee of the Chambers suppressing the Jesuit
Orders, the Ministers will hold a Cabinet
Council to consider the course to be followed
by the Government. It is expected that Sing
Victor Emmanuel will preside at the Council.
The vote of the Private Committee has been
received with great favour by the anti-Jesuit
party at the Vatican.

In Bern it is proposed to build a Natural
Historical Museum. In order to supply the
necessary capital, the Burgergemeinde has re-
solved to grant 200,000 francs out of the reserve
funds of the Deposit Bank.

Police-constable Brown, who was sentenced.
to a month's imprisonment at the Hammer-
smith Police-court, was released from con-
finement on Monday morning at seven o'clock.
He was the first constable who was sentenced
to imprisonment for having taken part in the
late police mutiny. It was for gong to hear
his ease tried that the men of the P, or Carter-
street division of police were disoharge4. It
is said that a large sum of money has been
collected for Brown's benefit.

Major Palliser, of chilled-shot renown, is to
receive from her Majesty the honour of knight-
hood.

Her Majesty the Queen, accompanied by
their Royal Highnesses Prince Leopold and
Princess Beatrice, left Windsor on Tuesday
morning, by special train, for Gosport, ea rout°
for Osborne.

Mr. Horace Greeley's sister, MN. J. F.
Cleveland, is lying very ill at her residence,
in Cottage-place, New York, the result of the
shock of her brother's death.

A sad ice accident is reported from Hamilton,
where four young colliers, who had ventured
upon a pond near Lesmahagow Junction, on
Sunday, were drowned.

A requisition has been 'sent to Lord Fermoy,
Lord Lieutenant of Cork, to convene a meeting'
in favour of the purchase of the Irish rail-
ways by the State.

James Jones, who described himself as a
"general dealer," was charged on Monday at
the HighgatiPoice-court with enteriur, ou the
18th ult. the residence of the Lord entering
while his lordship was at dinner, and stealing
jewellery, &0., of the value of .2250. The
police, having a clue to prisoner's accomplice,
asked for a remand, which was granted..

A navvy, named 11I'Innes, has been appre-
hended and lodged in prism at Lanark, pend-
ing investigation into the circumstances
attending the death of his wife at Carluke.
The woman died on Saturday from injuries
sufficient in themtelves to cause her death,
and it is alleged that she was assaulted by her
husband the previous night.

The guardians of Kensington parish have
decided to give a Christmas dinner to the in-
mates of the workhouse at a cost of is. Bd. a
head. Permission has been granted to the
lady visitors to give a tea to the inmates of the.
infirmary; and a balance in hand of £6 18s4
remaining from last year will be spent upon
entertainments for the children at the dif-
ferent parish schools.

A serious fire occurred in St. Andrew'
Church, Southport, on Sunday night. Before
the flames were extinguished the organ was
destroyed, and a portion of the stonework
surrounding the organ chamber much damaged.
,The loss is estimated at between £l,OOO and
£1,500. It is supposed that the fire originated
from the overheating of the warming apparatus.

kmeeting was held on Monday at the London
Tavern, with the object of forming a society
to provide the working class and persons of
small means with the various surgical ap-
pliances at a reasonable price, and on easy'
terms of payment. A resolution in favour of
the proposal was agreed to; and a committee
nominated to form the society.

Oa Tuesday the Streets Committee brought
up a report on the subject of street watering
by means of small jets from leaden pipes laid
along the footways, and recommending that
Mr. Brown be allowed to try his method of
watering in Princes-street, at his own expense;
upon condition that, if required, he reraove
his appliances and make good the pavement to
the satisfaction of the engineer, without sost
to the commissioners. The recommendation
was agreed to.

In an action to recover damages for breach
of promise of marriage, which was heard in
the Court of Exchequer on Tuesday, the plain'
tiff was the daughter of a licensed victualler,
and about 22 years of age, while the de-
fendant was a year or two older, and a teacher
of music! at Liverpool. Baron Martin, in the
course of the hearing, expressed an opinion
that, as the young lady had returned the
defendant's letters, she had exonerated him
from the promise which he had given her. By the
consent of counsel a juror was then withdrawn,
and the case cgme to an abrupt conclusion.

At Tuesday's sitting of the Central Criminal
Court, the charge of libel against Mr. John
Hampden,. brought by Mr. Alfred Russell
Wallace, again came nuclei the consideration
of Mr. Commissioner Kerr. It was stated that
Mr. Hampden, whilst professedly apologising
to Mr. Wallace had repeated observations of
a libellous character. The Commissioner
therefore ordered a fresh apology to be pub-
lished in the newspapers once a week until
next session, and warned the defendant that
if there were "any more nonsense" about the
reservation of legal rights he must put the law'
in force, should the order of the Court not be
carried out.

Dr. Brewer, M.P. for Colchester, has been
attack:ed, while on a tour in Italy, with a fever
described as " gastric rheumatic, of a remittent
typhus character." The hon. gentleraan
now recovering, but convalescence is not rt
established.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Wednebdai
morning, William Anderson, a raercheot,
carrying on business in Liverpool, Greenock,
and other towns, was found guilty of forging
acceptances on an extensive scale and Was
senteuced to five years' penal servitude.

Reckless speed on the part of a mail-cart
driver, whereby: two persons sustained serious
injuries, was visited at the Central Criminal
Court with a sentence of six months' hard
labour—the Deputy-Recorder refusing to ac-
cept the plea that duty obliged the prisoner, as
it seems to oblige also so many of his colleagues,
to put in peril the lives of foot-passengers.

On Tuesday evening an inquest was held at
Aldershot on the body of Hospital-Sergeant
Mawle, of the Ist Royal Scots. The decease&
was apprehended as a deserter, and was being
conveyed by two of the mounted military
police to the Second Brigade guard-house,
when he attempted to escape. One of the
provosts called out that if the deserter did not
stop he would ride him down. The sergeant
still persisting in his attempt, the provost rode
over him and broke both his legs. The jury
found a verdict in accordance with these facts.
An inquiry had already been held at the
Camp, at which the provosts were exonerated
from all blame.

Snow fell in Bradford on Monday night,
and lay to an average depth of six inches.
It thawed rapidly, and was followed, by a
thick fog, shops, mills, and warehouses being
lighted up as at night. Telegraphic coin-
munioation has been seriously interrupted by
the breaking down of the wires, and railway
traffic is also much delayed.

s A collision occurred on Monday morning
between the 8.15 express from Southport to
Manchester and a coal train, at Pendleton, on
the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. The
coal -train was standing on the main line wait-
ing the signal to proceed to Manchester. At
the same time the express, which was running
at a great speed, made its appearance in the
distance. The driver of the coal train started
his engine, but he had not gone far when the
express dashed into the rear of his train. Four
or five of the coal trucks were smashed to
atoms; and the driver of the coal train was
thrown from his engine, which ran along the
line and came into collision with a goods train
near the Oklfield-road Station in Salford.
Traffic was delayed for some hours, but in
neither collision was much further injury done
except to the rolling stock.

On Tuesday the remains of Lady Doughty
were interred in the family mausoleum at
Tiohborne. The coffin bore the inscription—
" Prayfor the repose of the soul of Mary,
Katherine, daughter of James, ninth Lord
Arundell, of Wardour, and widow of Sir
Edward Dbughty, Baronet, who departed this
life Dec. 12, 1872. Aged 77 years." High mass
was performed in the private chapel at eleven
o'clock by the Right Rev. Bishop of South-
wark.

At the conclusion of the adjourned inquest
on the body of the woman Sarah Hooper
Martin, suspected to have been murdered near
New Hampton a fortnight ago, the jury found
that she • died from having her throat out,
but how such injury was caused there was no
evidence to show." At the wish of the jury
a-recommendation to offer a reward was com-
municated to the Home Secretary by the
coroner.

Various plans for a reform of the Prussian
Cabinet seem to have been put forward in
consequence of Prince Bismarok's threat to
withdraw from the Premiership ; and one, to
which" special prominence" is said to be given,
would almost appear to have been framed in
the view of averting an incident that cannot
be too welcome at the Royal Court. The
scheme involves the re-establisbment of the,
old post of Prussian Chancellor of State, under
whom, as supreme authority saving the Crown,
the Minister-President and all his colleagues
would be placed.

• Reports continue to reach us of the destruc-
tive effects of the gale in the North. From
the mouth of the Tyne northward a lament-
able loss of life has occurred. On Wednes-
day eyening the gale raged with great fury
at 'Wick. In the midland counties the flood
still prevail, but fortunately there has been
/3 oareely any
_rainfall during the last twenty-
our hours.

A desperate assault was committed on. Tues-
day evening on a man named Michael Mahee,
at Barnagloe, near Nenagh. He was beaten
with stones, and had his skull fractured. A
man named Kelly has been arrested. ,

A. young lady of respectable familY, living
pear the South Circular-road, Dublin, at-
tempted to commit suicide on Tuesday, by
throwing herself out of window. Her mother
saved her.

Prom April let to the 14th inst., the Ex-
chequer receipts amounted to £48,798,537, as
compared with £46,587,220 in the correspond-
ing period of last year. The expenditure has
been £48,406,404. On Saturday lait the
balance in the Bank of England exceeded
£6,000,000 sterling, _

Denis Byrne, a builder in a respectable way
of business in Liverpool, was found guilty at
the Liverpool Assizes of perjury, on 'Wednes-
day. ' For three successive years he had sworn
to the ownership of property as a qualification
which he had really sold. The judge (Mr.
Kay, Q.C.), commented with great severity
upon the case and upon the prevalence of per-
jury in the Lancashire Courts of all kinds. It
was a wonder to him how in Lancashire one
man could believe another's word. Byrne
was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment
with hard labour.

-- •
The heavy rains of the past few days have
had the effect of inundating all the low-lying
lands in the neighbourhood of Worcester.
During Monday night the Severn rose as much
as nine feet, and all the adjacentmeadows were
completely submerged. On Tuesday morning
a flock of about forty sheep in a field belonging
to Mr. Essex, farmer, Leigh Sinton, were
swept away by the river Tome, and the shep-
herd, in his attempt to save one of them which
trad got eptangled in the hedge, was carried
off by the flood and drowned.

Addresses and letters of condolence are
pouring in from every part of the kingdom
and from every class, showing the respect in
which the late Lady Beaconsfield was held,
and the universal aesire to afford proofs of
sympathy with her illustrious husband.

About twenty tons of chalk cliff fell near
the Abbott Cliff early on Tuesday morning.
A stAff of men were immediately dispatched
from the Dover station, who in a very short
time cleared the line of the rubbish, thus pre-
venting any delay to the traffic. A few tons
of chalk again fell. at East Cliff during the
night. No further damage to property was
caused.

Mr. Heny Blagrove, the eminent English
violinist, died on Sunday evening at his
residence in London, after a lengthened and
severe illness. The immediate cause of his
death was congestion of the lungs, but he had
suffered from a oontplication of maladies, and
his ease had for some time- been regarded as
hopeless.

Four stokers, employed by the Kingston
Gas Company were summoned on Wednesdily
morning before the Kingston borough magis-
trates for leaving their work without Uotiee.
Attracted by the higher wages in London
during the stlike, they engaged themselves to
the Equitable Gas Company. The Bench cam-
mitted them eackto 14 days' hard labour.

Mr. Robert Bowles, the American banker,
who had been detained in Newgato on Tuesday
night, in consequence of a difficulty having
arisen respecting his bail, on Wednesday
released the next day, his solicitor haying
produced three gentlemen as sureties in the
sum of £4,000.

A man named Edward Hancock was indicted
at the Warwick Assizes on Wednesday for the
wilful murder of his wife, whom he had
occasionally ill-treated, through a feeling of
jealousy. He was found guilty, and sentenced
to death.

An inquest was held on Wednesday upon
the body of Daniel Moriarty, an Irish labourer,
45 years of age, who was attacked by his wife
with a hatchet on the night of Saturday, the
7th instant, and died in King's College
'Hospital a week afterwards. Evidence was
given to show that both the prisoner and the
deceased were addicted to drink, and that the
woman was in a state of semi-intoxication
when she committed the crime with which
she is charged. The jury returned a verdict
of wilful murder against her, and she was com-
mitted for trial. -

At Woolwich Police-court, a flue of forty
shillings, or one month's imprisonment, was
inflicted on a man, recently employed at Bec-
ton gas works charged with assault and in-
timidation in connection with the gas strike.

"Wilful murder" was the verdict returned
on Wednesday night by the coroner's jury
against Anne Moriarty, who some days age
inflicted on ,her, husband, in Drury-lane, in-
j uriesof which he has sines died in the hospital.
Before the finding at the inquest the womp
had already been committed for trial at Bow-
street Police-court.

Five hundred guests including some of the
most brilliant and distinguished names in the
list of our aristocracy, were present at the
grand ball in honour of the Prince and

SOW ENGLAND_ DEALS WITH HER

POOR.

Triz ease of Imams SrursoN; who was
charged before Sir ROBERT CARDEN the other
day with begging, but who turned out to be a

respectable poor woman who sought charity in
the streets because she was refused relief by
the authorities of St. Olive's, Southwark, un-
less she and her family went into the work-
house, at the risk of becoming permanent
paupers, is a case worth more than a passing
thought.
The husband of this poor woman is an in-
dustrious man, in daily expectation of em-
ployment, so that the difficulty was to
,tide
over the evil time until the work came, with-
out his family suffering absolute starva-
tion. There must be many such cases, and
there ought to be no difficulty in furnishing
the necessary relief; but somehow or other
those who administer our poor laws seem bent
on making them harsh and degrading; and in
such oases as the above seem as if disposed to
make them aggravate the evil they have to
deal with.

We have before called attention to the meet-
ings of guardians which have been recently
discussing questions connected with the ad-
ministration of relief, and we have pointed out
that the whole thought of these people seems
to be how they shall so frighten the poor as to
prevent them from seeking relief. The Poor Law
Amendment Act of 1834 tried to out down
expenditure by insisting that applicants should
go into the "house," and when there, they
made their lives so wretched that they were
glad to get out, even at the risk of dying by
starvation. Asa matter of course, the rates
ran rapidly down, to the delight of rigid
economists; but in a little time they began to
run up again, until they had reached their old
point, and under every trial that has been
made, whether local and general, the same
result has always been brought out.
_ .

In truth, we have a certain number of in-
firm people—improvident and lazy people—
unfortunate people who cannot procure em-
ployment, and who, therefore, cannot get food
—and young people, who are dependent on
those, and who, under all circumstances, must
fare as they fare,—who are born to an inherit-
ance of pauperism as the children of rich
people are born to affluence and luxury.
Millions sterling are paid every year for the
support of these in idleness. No effort is
made to employ the able-bodied, or to train
the young so as to fit them for the every-day
labours and duties of life. Can any living
mania his senses say why this is so? Why
is this open gulf always yawning for its annual
tribute? The thousands who are shut up in
our poor houses and prisons, teeny nothing of
our army and navy, all whom the State must
provide in food and clothing, could not but
furnish a constant market for whatever could
be produced by the organization of the labour
of these idle people, and this organization in
turn would furnish an excellent training school
for the young, so as to iit them, in'overy way,
to become good citizens or emigrants, who
would be welcomed in any direction in which
they might turn their faces.
Our whole system of poor laws is a' mockery
of common sense—a stupendous instance of
national folly. We breed our paupers as
vermin are bred amongst filthy people, indif-
ferent to the virtues of soap and water. These
wretched people are in the hands of the
Government, to do what they will with them,
or for them by insisting on wise legislative
provisions in the administration of the law.
Any amount of money may be raised for the
purpose of carrying out any well-considered
plan for their improvement, and yet we have
nothing but the old annually recurring demand.
The old filthy sore, so much got every year,
and so much spent every year, and there the
matter ends. Can Mr. STANSFELD do nothing?
If so, what businesd' has he where he is?
Whig and Tory, in this matter, are alike.
Would it not be well if our working men t:ied
to see what ought to be done, and insist on
our Government, whatever its complexion,
attending to it, and doing it without any
further loss of time? It is true our paupers
will not go into revolt, but there hi no know-
ing what may come out of the conditions which
breed our paupers, and whioh keep in misery
millions who yet rank amongst our indepen-
dent workers.

Mr. LOWE solemnly assured las audienoe the
other day at Swindon, that though law can do
many things, the putting down of orime and

poverty is beyond its power, and that to look
for such a power in law is to encourage in the
public) mind tendencies towards socialism.
But we beg to inform the OrraNcELLon of the
EXCHEQUER that nobody asks the Government
to attempt such a task. We believe as strongly
in the incompetency of the Government for
such a work as Mr. LOWE himself can. What
is complained of is that no practical experi-
ment of any kind is tried to improve per-
manently the character and administration of
our poor laws. Poverty, perhaps, must con-
tinue, do what we may, but that is no reason
against trying something effectual to check
it. On the contrary, it is a very strong reason
why the money collected for its relief should
be spent in a more useful manner than at
present. People will not continue to be
frightened by the bugbear of "socialism."
And in using such a phrase, Mr. LOWE proves
that he is not above resorting to the mere vulgar
tricks of party he which charged against his
opponents. The Tories may be as sordid as
he says they arc; no doubt the possessors of
office and aspirants to office know each
other's motives pretty well, and have many
reasons for abusing each other roundly; but
whatever may be done in this way, Mr. LOWE
is the last man who ought to make such
charges. His own conduct in regard to the
last Reform measure, added to what he has
done since, stamps him as a man without one
particle of principle, without an atom of poli-
tical honesty; and he is beneath contempt as a
mere political charlatan, when he flings charges
of political corruption from one hand, and
imputations of" socialism" from the other.

articles.title: CONSERVATIVE TEACHING.
articles.text:
CONSERVATIVE TEACHING.

THE Conservative, a paper written and
printed for the benefit of the working men of
England, contains this week an item or two
of information and advice which indicate the
benefits likely to be received by those who
attend humbly and confidingly to its teachings.
Through suoh a channel home Ad foreign
news will flow out upon the country so care-
fully prepared as to contain no properly dama.
ging to the loyalty of the people, and from
Bluth a source instruction will be furnished eel-
oulated to destroy the influence of" agitators,"
and all others who disturb public content, or
who in any way seek to destroy the belief of
those well-to-do people who assert• that in
Great Britain everything is as well as it can
be. The first paragraph to which we call
attention runs thus:—" It is terrible to think
that M. Timm' unwillingness to co-operate
unswervingly with the Conservatives is
founded upon the fear that if he does the
Republicans will make him pay for what they
represent as his desertion of them with his
life." This is not gtven as a joke, but in the
gravest way possible, and is made to carry a
fair amount of instructive comment which
cannot fail to have its due effect on the
operative Conservative mind.
The next point occurs in a leading article
on the Exeter Hall Labourers' meeting.
In mentioning the substitution of Sown
MORLEY for Sir SIDNEY WATERLOW as
chairman, it speaks of Sir SIDNEYaS "a chair-
man whose name, whatever his political errors,
is known for his practical services to the work
ing classes, was exchanged for a political
agitator." Our readers are to note for the
future that SA/iIIIEL MORLEY is to be regarded
as a political agitator, no doubt deluding the
people for the purpose of living on their labour.
After dealing with men and things in
this judicious and discriminating way, through
nearly three columns, it becomes patronising
and begins to advise: "If the union, of whieh
Mr. Anon is the chief, will remember this, if
they will strive to provide for their superfluous
men ,not by forcing them on the farmers through
the compulsory idleness of the employed, but
by sending them elsewhere, they may succeed,
and even ultimately be on good terms with the
farmer." Our contemporary, the Conservative,
has not yet cut its eye teeth. It gives its
advice without knowing what it is talking
about. lithe gentlemen who write in it knew
a little more of the world in which they live
—if they had, even in the most casual way,
noticed the proceeding of the Labourers 'Union,
they must have known that this is the work
, which occupies most of their attention, and

which they carry forward with most energy.
If our contemporary gives such advice as this
often, even the blindest and most benighted
operative Conservative will begin to suspect
that it is spending its juvenile energy very
uselessly in "teaching its grandmother to suck
eggs," as there must be a limit even to the
extent these poor fellows can be imposed on.
An operative Conservative, after all, is "a
man and a brother," and ought not to be
treated as if he had absolutely parted with his
understanding.

The views of our contemporary on the land
question can admit of no doubt, and arc worth
quoting literally—" If a landowner deliberately
prefers to use his property in one way rather
than in another, we should like to know how
it is proposed to compel him to devote himself
to what others may consider to be his best

interest?" In other words, oanhe not do what

be likes with his own? We do not ask opera-
tive Conservatives what they think of such
teaching as this, inasmuch as vie have no
reason to believe that they trouble their heads
much in thinking of anything connected with
our abstruser political questions. These law-
loving gentlemen, who call their neighbours
spoliators, and who want poor men to crawl
before authority and law, desire that the land-
owners should be above its power. We say,
on the contrary, they never were, and they
never can be. We do not say the law should
deal unjustly or harshly with them, but we
insist that in the mode of letting their estates,
and of managing those estates in reference to
the well-being of the nation, the law can, and
will, prescribe the rules by which they must
be guided. Great Britain is a nation, not a
number of private estates, and every separate
individual interest must submit to such regu-
lation as the general welfare may call for.
How far this doctrine shall be carried, or what
way it may be worked out, must depend on
public opinion, and the requirements of the
country at any particular time. If a land-
owner, or rather a "landholder," should at
any moment think proper to turn the whole of
his estate into a great game preserve, and so
render it necessary for the people to swarm off,
a remedy would soon be found in the law to
correct such an abuse of individual right; and
the Conservative may rest assured that any-
thing it could urge to Prevent this in its
juvenile flippant way would be laughed at by
men earnestly and soberly bent on the pre-
servation of the nation's life in its unity and
strength.

articles.title: M. THIERS AND THE THIRTY.
articles.text:
M. THIERS AND THE THIRTY.

TIIE politicians of Versailles and Paris are
puzzled by the long speech made by M.
Trims before the Committee of Thirty.
They find it strewed all over with sentences
or phrases of so subtle a character that their
meaning either cannot be penetrated at all, or
may be taken as the hearers or the readers are
inclined. The real explanation lies, no doubt,
in the situation of the man; and the sincerity
of his intentions must be set, by way of
apology, if not of justification, against the
managing propensities of the man.
Does he abandon the policy declared in his
Message? Does he endorse that speech of his
MINISTER of JusTlez which gained a vote in
the Assembly? Or does he, after all, adhere
to a line of policy to which, without a great
modification of their principles and objects,
the major part of its members cannot reconcile
themselves? Such are the main questions for
the solution of which this way or that French-
men are anxiously waiting. It will not do to
be guided by the tone of party and faetioniet
journals in reference to these momentous
matters. These make the words of the PRESI-
DENT of the REPUBLIC mean what they wish;
and, if while one finds in it an abandonment
of the Message, another interprets it
as a re-affirmation of what that document
contains, observers, free from bias, are
naturally thrown upon their own powers of
discrimination for a right judgment in the
ease. In the meantime, the whole question
is one as to which mere trimming, how skil-
fully 'mover performed, cannot possibly answer
in the end.

He said in the Message, that the Republic,
is the lawful government of the country, in
which, he added, Monarchy is not now poi-

ble. Has he, in the speech, retracted either
of these assertions? By no construing can it
be made out that he has. On the contrary,
the speech runs parallel with the Message.
Every one, in or out of France, very well
knew that he did not affect to settle for an
everlasting future. That were beyond human
power anywhere, most of all in fickle France.
It will be for the three Monarchical factions
to settle among themselves, or each for itself,
in what part of that age of ages their com-
bined or their separate chances are to come.
These chances, however, must occur at no
great distance from the present time, if M.
GIMBETTA'S " experienced old man " is to have
anything to do with either their realization or
their disappointment. Ho said in his Mes-
sage, that the Republic exists without any
necessity to proclaim it; and he adds in his
speech, that it is necessary, and even urgent,
to consolidate the institutions of the Republic
forthwith.

Of course, as he once more allows, he is
only the delegate of the Assembly; and this
has been described as a piece of affected
humility; but it can hardly have been designed
ivith this view, and cannot by the softest man
of the majority be interpreted as an act of
deference real or pretended, since it is closely
coupled with a clear avowal, that, if he is to
govern with success, he must have an increase
of power. As charged., with the Executive in
the most trying times, he will not endure to
be reduced, as the majority would reduce him
under their notion of Ministerial responsibility
to the position of a mere First Minister, whom
a hostile vote may, at any factiously selected
moment, force into resignation and retirement.
in plain terms, he will not suffer them to shut
his mouth and bar him out of the tribune, on
any other condition than the enactment of a
series of measures having for their aim and
effect the regularisation of the Government of
the Republic, and that in a definitive form.
Members of the majority showed that they,
at any rate, were no novices in the arts of
affectation, when, as an inducement to M.
LITERS to accept exclusion from the tribune,
they professed a deep solicitude to spare so
venerable a man the pain of hearing himself
spoken of in a disagreeable manner. He soon
told them in reply, that he, like another
leader, had not been these forty years in the
wilderness without becoming case-hardened
against such unpleasantnesses ; and ho might
well have taken so much kindness as a pretty
clear intimation that, if once his back were
turned upon them, they would not spare him
in his absence.

It is remarkable, that, while speaking again
of a series of constitutional measures, the only
such measure of which M. TuiEns now made
specific mention was the constitution of a
Second Chamber. He excused himself for the
bareness of this single suggestion, by the plea,
that he could not then and there go beyond
generalities. It remains, therefore, in his own
bosom, of what materials he would compose his
Second Chamber, what form he would give to
it, and with what degree of authority and class
of functions he would invest it. He could not
finish without adverting to the question of
Dissolution. If, on this head, he was too wary
to commit himself, the perpetuists, as one may
style them, have little to console them in what
he said. At least, lie treated the Dissolution
as disposed of, not conclusively, but only for
the present. He could have adopted no surer
method of multiplying petitions to the As-
sembly and addresses to himself. Meanwhile,
ho is open to an agreement with that body as
it now stands, on the means of constituting,
whether they and he like it best or not, a prac-
tical, useful, and workable Republic. Whatever
room may be found or imagined for a double
meaning in other sentences of the speech, it
concluded in terms which neither the committee
nor the Assembly, neither Frenchmen nor
foreigners, need be at any loss to understand
and appreciate. If, he said, the committee
would like to see him again and confer with
him on this basis, he would be very happy to
attend them; but he did not want any more
interviews for the mere exchange of reciprocal
courtesies. And, if the Collimate should de-
cide not to treat with him on the footing
mentioned, his only course would be to ask ,
the Assembly to decide between him and them.

We are of oiiinion, that the majority were
neither hoodwinked nor subdued. by M.
DUFAURE ; that, none the less on account of
the seeming tone of that Minister, M. TRIERS
abides by the plain substance of his Message;
that M. GAIkIBETTI is reaping the reward of
his masterly self-control; and that the ten-
dency to fusion between the Right and Left
Centres indicjates a fear lest the Republic
should take a more thorough and settled form
than M. TRIERS ever had any wish to give it.
In the country, fight will be made by a
league between place-hunters and priests.

articles.title: WARWICKSHIRE LABOURERS 1N THE
articles.text:
WARWICKSHIRE LABOURERS 1N THE

BRAZILS.

AT the Exeter Hall meeting, there -Were
some references to emigration as an alternative
to starvation for the agrfoultural labourers
who cannot live at home on such wages as
the farmers now pay. No sane man can desire
any thing like a sumptuary law dictating what
wages 'shall be given for any species of labour,
or even enacting that, for any particular
species of labour, such, for instance, as farm
work, a uniform rate of wages shall be paid in
every county and parish. It oanhardly be,
however, that any natural causes which politi-
cal economists can reduce to scientific rule,
should make it inevitable for the money earn-
ings of a Dorsetshire peasant to be no more
than half those of a Yorkshire "tiko," or even
less than that, But the main fact is that
which Messrs. BALL, MITCHELL, and ARCH
gave us; namely, that in their counties, wide
apart from each other, and, if not comprising
the highest rate of wages, yet not embracing
the lowest, the labourers cannot keep body and
soul together on the miserable price that land-
owner and landocoupiers in common now offer
them.

Mr. MonLEY, whose thorough earnestness
would be evident were it not proved by his
unequalled munificience, deprecated emigra-
tion on any large scale, not from mere dis-
like to the prospect of depopulating expatria-
tion, but from a persuasion that by migration
from one district of the country to another
honest work with bettor pay may yet be had at
home. Mr. Anal, on the other hand, who
has had some experience of the very thing that
the excellent CHAIRMAN so strongly favoured,
evidently fears that, whether they like it or
not, many thousands of the peasantry
will have either to die by inches at
home or seek a refuge and a liveli-
hood abroad. The practicable and avail-
able truth lies, as usual, between the two
opposites. Some relief may be found by mere
migration at home, and some by positive
emigration abroad. If we were to rely upon
the latter mainly or exclusively, much mis-
chief would be wrought by unavoidable delay
before the necessary machinery could be pro-
vided and set in motion. If the former altera-
tion were adopted as a sufficient relief under
the existing pressure, the process would be
found slow, at but gradual, perhaps, after al),
insufficient; and, in the meantime, the amount
of suffering would be intolerably groat.
While we are detailing the subject, a new
caution against rash experiments reaches us
from the central regions of the Am erican
continent. In May of this very year, a batch
of Warwickshire labourers listened to the
voice of the charmer, and are already repent-
ing of their easiness of faith. A professional
emigration agent turned up at the office-doors
of the Labourers' Union in Leamington. The
poor creatures who listened to his seductive
statements, were to be received on the
Brazilian shore by officers of the Imperial
Government, and, without any wandering
through the wilderness to be taken straight
to Cananea, which was held out to them as a
"Land of Promise," Small farms were to be
granted to each emigrant family, with tools
and seeds, and a daily allowance of two
shillings till the reaping of the first harvest.
To perfect the line, they were told that the
EMPEROR was struck with the Warwickshire
farming during his recent tour through
England, and had a special desire to form a
colony of such admirable peasantry within his
our dominions. As for mere labour inde-
pendently of farm grants, all who chose were
to have four shillings a day for six months,
and double afterwards, every man to work "at j

what he liked." The daily bill of fare was to
be no less attractive than the rate of wages,
including such delicacies as "duck, fowl, and
eggs." To crown all, a daily journal in
Birmingham made itself responsibh for giving
assurances that the soil covered inexhaustible
quantities of valuable minerals from gold to
lead, only wanting a road to the nearest port
to make them available to commerce, while
the liberality of the Government would add
a hundred per cent. in cash to whatever the
immigrants might spend upon their own
cottages.

As usual, the poor people out of Warwick-
shire and Oxford who listened to and relied
upon these fair-seeming promises report a
dreary deficiency of "milk and honey" in
the Canaan they were led to expect. Sum-
marising the doleful accounts already sent
home, the deluded voyagers found themselves
very badly treated. Even bread they had not
tasted, black beans and rice being the
substitutes for flour. They had not even
seen the acres they were to call their own.
Instead of clean and separate dwellings, they
were huddled together in hovels for which
pig-sties would be too good a name. Among
a total of one hundred and fourteen souls,
there had been five deaths in three weeks.
On landing they had to walk twelve miles, up
to their knees in mud, and lie all night under
no covering but torrents of rain. In fact,
nothing that the agent and others told them
had come true. One of the men, who prays
that his brother will not join him in that
place of torment, declares that he had been
undressed only three times since he turned
his back upon Banbury. Another of the
"Independent Landlord Farmers" that were
to be, writes home that it would cost him a
pound a day to live in this land flowing with
milk and honey, even as well as he was living
when induced to leave his cottage in Warwick-
shire. Mr. MOItLEY will do a useful service
if ho will apply to Earl Cins-Nvrt.f.o for an
inquiry into the extent to which the Brazilian
Government is responsible for the heartless
deception practised in its name. The suffer-
incurred will not have been all thrown away
if it makes the labourers listen with more
caution to speculators in the distresses of their
fellow creatures. Those who may have con-
tributed to enable the poor fellows to cross the
ocean into this atrocious trap, are now be-
sought to enable them to get out and come
home again. This is miserable work. The
agricultural labourers must take care and lose
no friends. They will want all they can find.

articles.title: FRENCH REPUBLIC.
articles.text:
THE FRENCH REPUBLIC.

A CAREFUL perusal of the great debate in
the French Assembly last Saturday gives
little hope of a peaceful settlement of the
matters at present in dispute in that distracted
country. Torn as it is by parties, no one of
which can prove its absolute predominance,
and neither of which will give way in the
interest of the country, it is difficult to see any
way out of the present difficulty, except by
force; and when the day comes upon which
the sword is to be drawn anew in civil strife,
the conflict will be deadly and terrible. The
disasters of the Commune, suffared as well as
done; the subsequent revenge of Versailles,
and all else that gives horror to French
history within the last hundred years, will be
trifling to the fierce hate and savage slaughter
by which the new struggle will be almost
necessarily characterised. The coming struggle
will not be purely political. The inten-
sity of anger felt by Royalists for Repub-
licans will be raised to a white heat
of madness by the clergy, who, in tho pro-
gress of popular liberty on the Continent,
see only the destruction of their power
as a class; and as the maintenance of this
power has always been the main object of their
lives, they will fight for it with the desperation
of despair.
Nothing can be more clear than that the
Right, or Conservative party, in the Assem.
bly do not mean now, and never did
mean, anything but the establishment of
a Monarchy. At first the rival ambi-
tions amongst themselves prevented this
design from being consummated during the
period of the worst confusion in the nation's
affairs. They feel now, however, that they

DEC. 21,

must act, and as they know the best field cf
action is in the Assembly, they will remain'
there and plot, until the country, by sheer force
or by an overwhelming expression of opinion,
compels them to forego their usurped functions.
If the Right is under the belief that it ought
to disregard the country, or if it pursues its
present course in a pretence of that belief, the
patience of the nation will be sorely tried.
If petitions pour in, and it is continued to,be
asserted, that they are promoted solely by
"agitators," such a course can have no other
effect but to exasperate those who send them.
If the Assembly accepts fully the statement
made by M. DURIURE on behalf of the Go-
vernment, to the effect that the sovereignty
of the people was only to be admittbd
on election day, and that "afterwards that
sovereignty was delegated to the Assembly,
which was a far better judge than the pea"
tioners could be as to when its career of
usefulness was over." Nothing but mischief
can come of it. We have here asserted the
right of Oe Assembly to continue its labours
as long as it can see in them anything which
it may, in its self-complacency, believe to be
useful, or rather till it can mature the plot and
carry out the plans which will give to France
a throne and a crown, and place her again'
amongst the monarchical nations of Europe-- .
with the priest and the noble hand-in-hand,
rejoicing over the prostration of the people.
This would be a terrible dilemma for a great
nation like France, and before the Republi-
cans can accept this position we are quite We
they will choose war even to the knife.
The men of the Left are the defenders of
the de facto Government. In the country or
in the Chamber it is their duty to establish the
Republic. It is their duty to save the French
people from the intrigues of rival factions,
whose agreement in this struggle means, and
can only mean, the political and social ruin of
the masses of the people. We cannot believe
that GA..mnErra, LOUIS BLANC, and others, who
have been appointed
,the leaders in this diffi-
cult and dangerous contest will betray the
trust reposed in them. The growth of public
opinion on their side has been rapid, and the
Conviction that by a Republic only peace,
prosperity, and strength can be secured to the
nation, is every day gaining ground. These
men know best whether the death-grapple
ought to be postponed or precipitated. At any
rate, they have proved their willingness by an
appeal to universal suffrage to let the people:
speak for themselves. But if the Right,
assisted by the Government, defy the popular
will, dethrone universal suffrage, tind put a
parliamentary intrigue against the settled eon-
viction and passionate hope of the people, upon
their heads must rest the responsibility of snob
bloodshed as may follow.

From every court in Europe this struggle is
watched with intense interest. Nay, it ik
absolutely certain that those in power
in all our monarchies hate the thought
of it strong Republic being set up in their
centre. They know with what rapiditY
ideas are propagated. They know hot
futile it is to set barriers up against theta
Monarchs have never yet ban able to ostab...
lish an effectual quarantine against liberal
thought. As it is in thought, so it is in the
business of life, Nations adopt from each
other every improvement in the arts of war
, and peace, as a mere matter of self-preservation.
Even America is daily sending us improved
machinery for productive as well as for de-,
struetive purposes. The new form of govern'
ment, like everything else, will be imitated it
it answers. Nothing can prevent this, and a*
the hand-loom weavers plotted against the'
introduction of the steam-loom, so princes alla
dukes, and earls and lords, and all who profit
by them as hangers on, will plot and oPPOI3.
any improved system of government that
threatens to take from them the privileges, the
power, and the profit they derive from the
systems of government now existing.
In the present struggle the Republicaas of
France have to fight with external as well sa
internal enemies, with spiritual as well as
temporal influences. We hope sincerely, has"
ever, that this new birth of a nation nia7 be

articles.title: DISESTABLISFESIVT QIIEBTION.
articles.text:
THE DISESTABLISFESIVT QIIEBTION.

A public meeting to support Mr. Mill's
motion was held on Tuesday night at the
Lambeth Baths; Mr. Andrew Dunn in the
chair. Mr. J. Carvell Williams, the Rev. J.
Shaw, the Rev. G. Murphy, Mr. Broadhurst,
and other gentlemen were on the platform.
The Chairman, in opening the proceedings,
mid that in presidine, he did so with a feeling
of great responsibility, as the question was a
most important one. The subject they were
met to discuss was the privileges of the Es-
tablished Church of England. They had no
quarrel with prelacy or presbytery; they
merely wished, through the agency of their
Society, to obtain by law the religious equality
of all men of whatever denomination. It
Was on that account that they asked for the
disendowment and disestablishment of the
Church of England and Scotland. He had no
hostile feelings towards Episcopalians, and did
not wish to say a word to wound their feelings.
Mr. J. Carvell Williams then addressed the
meeting. He said that the course of the Non-
comformists had been one of steady progress
ever since the commencement of their exist-
ence. Years ago the cry of the Dissenters was
for toleration, and he referred to the prophecy
of Lord Stanhope, who said that if they then
asked it as a favour, they would soon demand it
as a right, and eventually reject it as an
insult.. Then they had secured religious
liberty, and some thought they had obtained
as much as they could wish. They now asked
for religious equality, a' term which had only
been invented during the last few years. By
religious equality they aid not mean a wish to
occupy the position in the State that the
Church now held. They did not wish for
seats in the House of Lords, and they did not
desire the Church revenues. Their 's was a
levelling down and not a levelling up policy.
They were not, and they never had been,
actuated by selfish motives. The only way
by which religious equality could be secured
was by the State letting religion alone. All
should have the benefit of the State's pro-
teotion, but the State's favour should not be
granted to one body. The creed of the society
was summed up in the phrase—" Let every
tub stand on its own bottom." After answer-
ing some of the observations recently made by
Mr. T. Hughes, M.P., at Birmingham, and
dwelling upon the comparative merits of the
Church and the Nonconforming body, Mr.
Williams concluded .a long and exhaustive
address by referring to the colonies and to
America as instances of the success of religious
equality.
The Rev. J. Shaw then moved a resolution
that a petition to the House of Commons be
adopted by the meeting, and signed by the
chairman in support of Mr. Miall's motion.
The resolution was seconded by Mr. Broad-
hurst, and carried unanimously.

Lord Derby, presiding at the annual meet-

On Wednesday morning, the -vulcanite and

Mr. Thos. Richards, a large mill owner at
Pontypridd, was killed on Wednesday in a
shocking manner. While inspecting the
premises his cloths were caught by a cog-
wheel, by which he was drawn into the
machinery, and before the engine could be
stopped his body was torn to pieces.

articles.title: LIBERAL MEETING AT CREWE.
articles.text:
LIBERAL MEETING AT CREWE.

On Monday evening, a public meeting of
the Crewe branch of the West Cheshire Liberal
Association was held in the Town Hall, Creive.
Mr. Eaton presided.
The Rev. W. A. Blake (Crewe) moved :

That this meeting, desirous of continuing its
unabated confidence in her Majesty's Government,
trusts that its coming action may witness a bold
and progressive policy in all that concerns the civil
and religious liberties of the people.
Mr. Martin Heath seconded. the resolution,
which was unanimously passed.
Mr. W. G. Latham (Sandbach), whose in-
troduction to the meeting as the future mem-
ber for Mid-Cheshire elicited the loud cheers
of the audience, moved the following resolu-
tion :
That, in the matter of parliamentary reform,
this meeting urges upon the Government the
necessity of at once making a redistribution of
seats, and of extending to counties the same fran-
chise which is now in force in boroughs ; and that
in the opinion of this meeting it is imperative, in
the general interest of the country, that there
should be a readjustment of the incidence of local
taxation, and a great reduction in the national ex-
penditure.
Mr. Teasdale seconded the resolution, which
was supported by Mr. Wilson, Manchester,
and passed unanimously.
Mr. Jefeoate (engineer) moved, Mr. McNeill
seconded, and Mr. George Potter supported
the following resolution, which was unani-
mously carried :
That this meeting, having seen the unjust pro-
secutions that have taken place under the provi-
sions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, urged
upon Parliament to repeal the said Act, as this
meeting considers there is sufficient power given
under the common law of this country for the
punishment of such offences as are contemplates
in the Act in question.

Mr. J. W. Fluddlestone' Q.C., and one of
the Conservative members for Canterbury, was
on Wednesday married to Lady Diana Beau-
clerk, dam-alter of the Duchess of St. Albans.
The ceremony was solemnised at All Saints,
Knightsbridge, by the Bishop of Winchester.

On Wednesday night, in the Central-hall,
Darlington, a publio meeting was held to
denounce the slave trade, and to strengthen
the hands of the Government in seeking its
suppression. Mr. Joseph W. Pease, the member
for South Durham, presided, and, in opening
the proceedings, spoke in the highest terms of
the abilities and personal character of Sir
Bartle Frere, saying that his appointment was
in itself a guarantee of the intentions of the
Government. The Rev. Charles New, of the
Livingstone Search expedition, and Mr. Ben-
jamin Millard. were among the speakers. Reso-
lutions, in accordance with the objects of the
meeting, were passed unanimously.

On Wednesday the jury, empannelled to
inquire into the death of Sarah Hooper
Martin, at New Hampton, returned an open
verdict, at the same time recommending that
a reward for the discovery of the supposed
murderer should be offered by the Home-

Some time ago a girl named Nancy M'llean
servant with Mr. Whittle, residing near
Bolton, was, it was said, enticed to a Roman
Catholic Refuge by her sister. Application
has since been made at the Refuge for M'lrean,
but the authorities refused to restore her.
The Bolton Board of Guardians thereupon in-
formed the Local Government Board of the
affair, but the reply was that the Board could
do nothing. An account was afterwards sent
to Mr. Newdegate, M.P. and at the meeting
of the Guardians on Wednesday letters were
road from Mr. Newdegate asking for the names
of the superior and priest of the convent, or
of the Bishop connected with it. He promised
to co-operate with the Board in assisting
Whittle to recover the girl. The Board re-
solved to place the necessary documents, Bce.,
at his disposal.

A public meeting was held in the Town
Sall, Birmingham, on Wednesday, in support
of the principles of the Liverpool Finatunal
Reform Association. M-. J. S. Wright pre-
sided, aud the speakers included Mr. Peter
rlylands LP., Rev. Arthur O'Neil, Mr. A.
Jones, Mr. Wm. Trant, and others. A reso-
lution was passed, approving of the principles
or the Financial Reform Association, and
pledging the meeting to support it by all
means in its power. It was resolved, "That
this meeting believes that the time has now
arrived when decisive steps should be taken in
Parliament towards financial reform." A.
petition was adopted ;pointing out the extra-
vagant expenditure of the country, and asking
Parliament to repeal the duties on articles of
food, pending a more complete system of re-
form.

The journals of Alsace announce that the
environs of Strasburg are completely inun-
dated, and that the rise of the 111 continues
in disquieting proportions.

articles.title: ODD FELLOWS' JUBILEE.
articles.text:
ODD FELLOWS' JUBILEE.

On Monday evening, the members of the
metropolitan districts of the Independent
Order of Odd Fellows' (Manchester Unity)
Friendly Society held their jubilee dinner at
the Bridge House Hotel, London Bridge, where
330 oda Fellows sat down to an excellent
dinner, served by Mr. Joseph Spencer. The
Lord Mayor presided, and there were present,
Mr. Avrton, M.P.; Mr. McArthur, M.P. ; the
Hon. E. L. Stanley, Mr. J. Locke, M.P,;
Colonel Beresford, M.P., &c. The company
included a number of artillerymen from Wool-
wich, in uniform.
Mr. John Locke, M.P., proposed the toast
of" The Manchester Unity of Odd Fellows,"
which he said had on the let of January last
455 districts, 3,975 lodges 458,159 members,
and a total income of £591,717, with an ex-
penditure of £413,158, leaving a balance of
£168,599.
Mr. Curtis responded.
_ _ _ _ _

'rue Lord Mciyor proposed "The Metro-
potitan Districts," which he said had 200
lodges, 20.,782 members, aud an accumulated
capital of £235,933.
Other toasts followed, and speeches were
made by Mr. Holmes, Mr. Dansie, Mr. Love,
Mr. Newman, Mr. Level, the Hon. Lyulph
Stanley, Mr. L Tompkins, Mr. T. N. Day,
and M. J. Munro.

articles.title: ECONOMY IN COAL.
articles.text:
ECONOMY IN COAL.

A sum of ,2500 having been placed at the
disposal of the Council of the Society of Arts,
for promoting, by prizes or otherwise, economy
in the use of coal for domestic purposes, the
Council have decided to offer prizes, including
the Society's Gold Medal and £5O, for each of
the following objects t— •
1. For a new and improved system of grate
suitable to existing chimneys as generally con-
structed, which shall with the least amount of
coal answer best for warming and ventilating
a room.
2. For a new and improved system of grate,
suitable to existing chimneys as generally con-
structed, which shall vvith the least amount of
coal best answer for poking food, combined
with warming and ventilating the room,
3. For the best new and improved system
of apparatus which shall, by means of gas,
most efficiently and. economically .warm and.
ventilate a room. . .

4. For the best new and improved, system
of apparatus which shall, by means of gas, be
best adapted for cooking, combined with
warming and ventilating the room.
6. For any new and improved system or
arrangements not included in the foregoing,
which shall efficiently and economically moot
domestic requirements.

The Liberals of South Warwickshire, alive
to the fact that there is more than a possibility
of a vancanoy shortly arising in the repre-
sentation of the division, held a meeting at the
Globe Hotel, Warwick, on Tuesday evening.
There was a numerous attendance of the
principal supporters of the party. It was
decided to contest the first vacancy that may
arise, and in the event of only one vacancy
occurring, as is anticipated, the Liberal candi-
date will be Sir Robert N. C. Handliton, Bart.,
K.C.8., of Avon's Cliff, near Stratford-on-
Avon.

At Wednesday's sitting of the Central
Cour, Samuel Hoy, a lad twelve years of age,
was convicted of having attempted to ad-
minister poison to his step-mother, and was
sentenced to ten years' penal servitude.
Eleanor Ey, 38 years of age, was found
guilty of having thrown a quantity of sul-
phuric acid upon her husband, with intent to
no him grievous bodily harm, and a sentence
of seven years' penal servitude was passed.

The Liverpool Mercury says that Mr. Glad-
stone has consented to deliver the prizes to the
pupils at the Liverpool College on Saturday
next. The Prime Minister, accompanied by
Mrs. Gladstone and other members of Ins
family, will_ come from Hawarden on Saturday
forenoon, probably reaching the Landing Stage
about eleven o'clock. The meeting at the
college is fixed for noon, and it is probable
that Mr. Gladstone will remain with his bro-
ther, Mr. Robertson Gladstone, at Court-bey
until Monday.

articles.title: LATEST INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

The steamer St. Louis, for New Orleans,
which sailed from Liverpool on Wednesday,
had on board 184 emigrants, principally farm
labourers from Leamington and Birmingham.
The annual delivery of the winter speeches,
and the presentation of prizes in conneetion
with the St. Paul's sehool took place on Wed-
nesday at the school in St. Paul's-ohurchyard,
the
,head master, the Rev. IL Kynaston,
presiding. A large number of visitors were
present.

The Emperor William has aceepted tho
invitation of the Czar, go that his Majesty will
proceed to Styetersbarg at the beginning of
net May.

At a special meeting of the Cambridge Town
Council, yesterday, a communication was
received from the Royal Agricultural Society,
in reference to the proposal to hold its meeting
for 1874 in that city.. It was resolved to in-
vite the Society, and to use every effort to give
the members a satisfactory reception.

A correspondent telegraphs that, at the
Warwick Assizes, yesterday, W. Warmington
was sentenced to five years penal servitude for
embezzling £l2 deposited in the Post Office
Savings Bank. The judge said the offence
was most serious, and an example must be
made.

The death is announced of Sir Malby
Crofton, Bart., of Longford House, county
Sligo. He is succeeded in-the baronetcy by
his eldest son, Henry Bliss Crofton, captain
in the Sligo Militia. Sir Henry was born in
July, 1833, and married, October 24r 1866,
Solphia' eldest daughter of Mr. Thomas Hors.
fall, of Burley Hall, Yorkshire.

The Calais train ran oft' the line on Wed-
nesday morning at Gonesse. Nine carriage*
were damaged, but none of the passengers
were injured.

Father Jandel, the General of the Domini-
cans, is dead. Father Jandel was the unre-
lenting enemy of Father Lacordaire, the most
"distinguished Dominican of his century, and
did his best in the course of his career to
assimilate his orders to the Jesuits.
Mr. Gosohen, M.P., First Lord of the Ad.
miralty, and Admiral. Sir A. 3ttilne, First
Naval Lord, proceeded to Dartmouth yester-
day, to present prizes to the naval cadets on
board the Britannia.

As a natural enough sequel to his recent
marriage' which has proved an event of such
interest to the dwellers in the Flowery Land,
The Emperor of China is saki to be about to
undertake an enterprise rarely precedented in
the annals of his predecessors, a progress in
state through his dominions.

A correspondent telegraphs that on Wed.
nesday evening, a much-frequented pathway,
close to Cambourne, West Cornwall, had just
been. traversed by a lady and a little girl,
when suddenly a pit opened close to their
heels, and in three minutes it had sunk into a
chasm sixty feet deep. The cause of the
occurrence was the falling in of rotten wood-,
work, which had been placed ever a shaft of
a long since abandoned mine.

A special telegram from Brussels says that
in some quarters of Ghent the water is three
feet high in the streets. The factories have
stopped work and the houses are flooded.
The distress among the inhabitants is great,
and in some parts they are obliged to travel
in boats. The whole country between Ghent
and St. Nicolas is a. lake. At Liege the Maas
is very high.

At the Town Hall, Sheffield on Wednesday
application was made on behalf of the licensed
viotuallers for an extension of time on Christ-
mas Eve to twelve o'clock, Christmas Day to
eleven o'clock Saturday in Christmas week to
twelve o'clock, Sunday following to eleven
o'clock, and the four succeeding days till one
o'clock in the morning. The bench said that
whatever might have been their inclination
in the matter, the law would not allow them
to grant the application, and, it was accord.
ingly refused.

Some alarming reports have been current
concerning the health of his Royal Highness
the Duke of Cambridge. It is authoritatively
stated, however, that these rumours have no
foundation whatever in fact. The Duke has
for some days past suffered slightly from gout,
but was on Wednesday enabled to take his
ordinary exercise.

Mr. Justice Quain was occupied at the Con.
tral Criminal Court on Wednesday, with the
trial of George Cannon, superintendent of the
Casual Ward of the St. Giles's Workhouse,
who was indicted for the manslaughter of a
child, to whom, with its mother, he had refused
admission on an inclement night, and whose
death was alleged to have been accelerated by
exposure to the weather. He was convicted,
and the learned judge sentenced him to twelve
months' imprisonment with hard labour.

TO JOSEPH ARCH.
COMMUNICATED BY MIES STURM
(Of Birmingham.)
Hold up, brave man, the battle is not done, ,
Nor the long conflict of the centuries won!
The storms of heathen tumult rage and roar,
But Christ Himself is wrestling for the Poor!
Hold to the rock of our Humanity,
The stars, within "their courses" fight for thee,
Wave unto wave, and flood to flood may call,
Hold to the common Father of us alt!
Against the eternal "cords" the rich may fret,
The Church her high vocation may forget!
Those are the true successors of the men
Who built the Church, who build her yct

again,—
By righting wrong, by helping the oppressed,
Giving the weary his appointed rest;
By preaching the eternal law, alone,
That the great human family is one,
That in our Saviour Christ there cannot be
Nor male nor female, no, nor bond nor free.
He works amiss who only works for pelf,—
And he who wrongs his neighbour, wrongs him-

self ;
Who teaches this, treads whore Apostles trod,
Yea treads the fiotprints of the Son of God;
And he who treads, through sorrow and decrease,
Shall find at last, though late, the Land of Peace.
Let Dultes deal out their noisy threats and blows;
Let landlords swear their worn-out English

ouths ;
Let Paul's successors, over prandial wine,
To drown and crush the poor man's cause corn-

bins;
Hold up, brave man! thy portion let it be
To relieve the oppressed—to set the captive free.
Well was it for the Bishop and his cause
That friends around accorded their applauee.
Well was it for the Bishop! Did St. E'atil
Sit at the feast, he'd cry," Thou whited wall!
Thou sitt'at on high, with lawiessness to war;
Thou teachest angry men to break, the law."
When England, all divided, split and riven,
Shall be but one in sight of earth and heaven;
When the long feud of rights shall cease to be;
Sex against sex—the bond against the free,
Rich against poor, and money against toil,
And common man shall own God's common soil;
When the long fight of selfishness shall cease,
And all our ancient disobrds end in peace;
When men shall live (God grant it soon may be)
In the broad light of perfect charity,—
Then, Joseph Arch, we shall remember thee!
